Second, in a selected-value, single-model experiment, emphasized judge rubrics produce consistent but modest increases relative to paired suppressed rubrics, demonstrating a plausible mechanism for training-time amplification. Third, in off-policy evaluations across 14 models, inference-time personalization increases inappropriate agreement, with the largest effect from matched user profiles placed directly before the query.

items.title: Consistency Is Not Correction: Separating Confidence, Abstention, and Recovery in LLM Agents
items.author: Khushal Sethi
items.content: A controller that resamples an answer, escalates to a larger model, or abstains is usually justified by a confidence signal. Three claims about such a signal do not follow from one another: it ranks answers (discrimination), it supports withholding some of them (selective prediction), and it changes an answer for the better (correction utility). We give an exact decomposition of the third into gated recoveries minus gated harms, which bounds whether a comparison can succeed before it is run: a gate that only replaces a proposal can act only where the base policy was already wrong, so the initial error count caps the discordant pairs any correct gate can produce. When that cap falls below the count a paired test needs, the experiment cannot return a positive result for a working mechanism, nor distinguish one from a gate that never fired. We measure all three targets on two model scales and find the bound binds. In a small-model suite a perturbation-agreement verifier reaches within-policy AUROC 0.990 (95% interval [0.95, 1.00]) while every episode outcome matches single-sample decoding at 4.32 times the call count. In a controlled 840-episode study no verifier replaced the proposal on any of the 60 GSM8K decisions, so that comparison tested nothing; the entire GSM8K gain across six controllers is one task, and it is the task whose identical temperature-zero repeats disagreed, making it the one answer the service does not reproduce. On the diagnostic set the gate could reach four errors while the test needed six, so even a perfect gate had no significant result available. We report two checks that would have caught this before any budget was spent, and show that tie handling in rankings, tied selection cutoffs, and unequal output limits each move a headline number in the same dataset. The binding constraint on this literature is measurement resolution, not the choice of signal.

items.title: Evaluating Semantic Insensitivity in Financial Sentiment Analysis: Implications for Sustainable Financial Decision-Making
items.author: Gabriela Cioboata, Teodor-Stefan Bildea
items.content: Financial sentiment analysis is critical for automated trading, portfolio management, and risk assessment, heavily relying on models like FinBERT. Despite high benchmark accuracy, these models remain vulnerable to subtle adversarial text modifications, threatening the integrity of algorithmic decision-making. In this paper, we propose Agent-driven Semantic Inversion (ASI), a novel adversarial attack framework targeting financial sentiment models through domain-specific semantic manipulation. Utilizing an LLM-powered multi-agent pipeline, our approach identifies eligible financial news sentences and applies targeted lexical substitutions. We empirically evaluate ASI against FinBERT, one of the most widely deployed financial sentiment models. Our results reveal a striking vulnerability: the attack successfully deceived FinBERT in 90.85% of eligible cases, with the model frequently maintaining its original sentiment prediction despite the fundamental inversion of financial performance indicators. Through qualitative analysis and token-level investigation, we demonstrate that FinBERT critically over-relies on contextual keywords and syntactic patterns rather than true logical comprehension of financial semantics. Our findings highlight the urgent need for logic-aware, robust financial NLP models to ensure the reliability of automated decision-making systems.

items.title: Token Commitment as a Control Surface for Steering Masked Diffusion Generation
items.author: Ambroise Aigueperse, Hugo Buurmeijer, Carmen Amo ALonso, Marco Pavone
items.content: Masked diffusion models repeatedly predict provisional tokens before a sampler decides which predictions become permanent. Existing inference-time steering methods primarily modify activations, logits, or denoising trajectories, while treating this commitment policy as a fixed decoding detail. We instead study token commitment as a diffusion-specific control surface and separate it into two decisions: which tokens to commit and how many tokens to commit at each step. For the first, we introduce counterfactual target-aware commitment, which ranks unresolved positions by a mixture of model confidence and leave-one-token-out target contribution. For the second, we introduce calibrated adaptive budgets driven by target progress and confidence. Across language and vision-language settings in the LLaDA family, multiple targets, two activation-steering methods, and an unsteered control, both mechanisms yield empirically monotonic target-quality trade-offs in every configuration we evaluate. Adaptive schedules also recover competitive operating points relative to scorer-free stochastic schedules matched in average denoising cost. Because both mechanisms require only a scalar score evaluated on a provisional completion, they apply unchanged when the target is an automatic proxy for task success rather than an output attribute: NLI entailment for dialogue summarization and CLIPScore for captioning, neither of which corresponds to a single reusable steering direction. We reproduce the behavior of both mechanisms on a second masked-diffusion family, Dream-7B, for one control target and one task-success target. These results characterize commitment--which provisional predictions become irreversible, and how rapidly--as an interpretable control surface for steering masked diffusion generation under the conditions we test.

items.title: NEBench R1: a Reasoning Benchmark for Evaluating Nuclear Domain Competence in Large Language Models
items.author: Liyan Wang, Longze Li, Mohamed Hassan, Isshu Lee, Dajie Sun, Ruimin Feng, Aleksandar Vakanski
items.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored for knowledge-intensive and safety-critical applications in nuclear engineering. However, existing nuclear-domain benchmarks provide limited content coverage or focus primarily on answer accuracy without systematically evaluating the quality of the underlying reasoning. This study introduces NEBench R1, a reasoning-oriented benchmark comprising 7,546 unique multiple-choice questions extracted from U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) reactor operator licensing examinations covering 18 nuclear facilities. Each question is classified according to the NRC Knowledge and Abilities catalogs and accompanied by an official explanation serving as a reference for reasoning evaluation. Six LLMs were evaluated, with overall accuracy ranging from 34.0% to 73.9% across three distinct performance tiers. To assess reasoning quality, an LLM-based judge evaluated correctly answered responses using a multidimensional rubric. Although responses generally demonstrated strong problem comprehension, they scored lower in factual and procedural accuracy and distractor analysis, indicating that correct answers were not necessarily supported by technically sound justifications. Response clarity was also weakly indicative of technical quality. Furthermore, longer reasoning traces were associated with lower accuracy in both frontier reasoning models, suggesting that reasoning length may reflect question difficulty rather than improved problem-solving performance. Reasoning-token consumption may therefore provide an additional signal for identifying potentially unreliable responses. NEBench R1 establishes a benchmark for evaluating both answer accuracy and reasoning quality, providing a foundation for assessing the domain competence and reliability of LLMs in nuclear engineering.

items.title: DeltaHarness: Self-Evolving Harnesses for Resource-Adaptive Tool Execution
items.author: Lecheng Yan, Jianze Lin, Xicheng Han, Xiantao Xu, Wenxi Li, Chenyang Lyu
items.content: Tool-using agents rely on execution harnesses to organize and schedule tool operations. The same task and resource description can conceal runtime conditions that reverse the latency ordering of valid execution plans. Resolving this uncertainty requires firsthand execution in the target setting. We introduce DeltaHarness, an execution-guided policy-search method that adapts agent harnesses from cold-start measurements. Its QHI loop uses the observed response to update runtime dispatch, revise physical plans, and select experiments for later proposals. An independent confirmation panel controls policy replacement. With fixed dispatch, a revised materialization policy reduces complete-delivery latency by 30.0% on one video-editing task across three fresh pairs. On held-out tasks, the evolved policies reduce latency by 8.2% relative to the best fixed plan in one seed and by 4.6% relative to the initial proposal in another.

items.title: AdaFlowLite: Scalable and Non-blocking Inference on Asynchronous Mobile Data
items.author: Sicong Liu, Fengmin Wu, Yuan Gao, Bin Guo, Zimu Zhou, Hongkai Wen, Zhiwen Yu
items.content: The rise of mobile devices equipped with numerous sensors, such as LiDAR and cameras, has driven the adoption of multi-modal deep intelligence for distributed sensing tasks, such as smart cabins and driving assistance. However, the arrival time of mobile sensory data vary due to modality size and network dynamics, which can lead to delays (if waiting for slow data) or accuracy decline (if inference proceeds without waiting). Moreover, the diversity and dynamic nature of mobile systems exacerbate this challenge. In response, we present a shift to \textit{opportunistic} inference for asynchronous distributed multi-modal data, enabling inference as soon as partial data arrives. While existing methods focus on optimizing modality consistency and complementarity, known as modal affinity, they lack a \textit{computational} approach to control this affinity in open-world mobile environments. % \sysname pioneers the formulation of structured cross-modality affinity in mobile contexts using a hierarchical analysis-based normalized matrix. This approach accommodates the diversity and dynamics of modalities, generalizing across different types and numbers of inputs. Employing an multi-modal lightweight Swin Transformer (MMLST), \sysname facilitates real-time and flexible data imputation, adapting to various modalities and downstream tasks without retraining. Experiments show that \sysname significantly reduces inference latency by up to 80.4\% and enhances accuracy by up to 62.1\%, while achieving nearly a 50\% reduction in energy consumption, outperforming status quo approaches. Also, this method can enhance LLM performance to preprocess asynchronous data.

items.title: TIBECG: Temporal Information Bottleneck for Lead-Specific Demographic Privacy in ECG Waveform Release
items.author: Tsai-Min Chen (Research Center for Information Technology Innovation, Academia Sinica, Taipei, Taiwan, RIKEN Center for Interdisciplinary Theoretical and Mathematical Sciences), Jun Seita (RIKEN Center for Interdisciplinary Theoretical and Mathematical Sciences)
items.content: Transmitting an electrocardiogram (ECG) waveform can expose demographic information beyond an intended diagnostic task. We evaluate TIBECG, an architectural temporal information bottleneck, on individual leads extracted from hospital twelve-lead recordings. A 2,302,337-parameter processor varies its latent length while retaining the same nine-score consistency objective, without age or sex labels in protector fitting. Across 6,386 recordings, ten folds, 12 leads and 21 lengths, retrospective selections retained at least 95% of each lead's clean macro-F1. Their weaker age/sex interval gain exceeded the best eligible conventional transformation on all leads, by a median 22.08 percentage points. The implemented sampling-rate comparison shows that direct downsampling usually suppresses demographic inference more strongly but at a larger loss of diagnostic utility, whereas TIBECG favors utility preservation. Selection stability also varies by lead. Lower latent Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence does not reliably rank residual sex leakage at a fixed length. These findings support lead-specific evaluation of waveform processing, not validated consumer deployment or expert-readable reconstruction. When the waveform-input diagnostic classifier is hosted as part of a proprietary cloud service rather than deployed on the device, waveform transmission is required to obtain its scores.

items.title: Layerwise Learning-Rate Scaling in Vision Networks: Effective-Rate Identification, Power-Mean Aggregation, and Budget Dependence
items.author: Chandini Vysyaraju, Raghuvir Duvvuri, Radu Timofte, Dmitry Ignatov
items.content: Layerwise learning-rate scaling assigns different learning rates to different parts of a network. Although established in fine-tuning pretrained models, its effects in vision networks trained from scratch are commonly assessed by training each candidate recipe. We show that, in this setting, the rate-related component of a layerwise strategy is well summarized by an effective learning rate computable directly from its multiplier profile. Across matched-control comparisons, changes in test accuracy closely track changes in training loss (r = -0.996), which supports an optimization-progress explanation of the short-budget rate effect. Increasing the untuned base learning rate tenfold shifts the rate-matched contrast upward in all six tested architectures (p = 0.016) and increases the number of architectures in which a published discriminative schedule, excluded from model fitting, outperforms the uniform control from two to five of six (p = 0.031). Within the evaluated strategy space, a parameter-weighted power mean with exponent 0.35 (95% confidence interval [0.20, 0.50]) accounts for 42.6% of within-architecture variance, compared with 36.4% for the arithmetic mean. Ranking candidates by this scalar without training improves the selected candidate's mean percentile rank from the 26th to the 10th and reduces its mean accuracy shortfall relative to the best candidate from 3.70 to 1.12 points. The rate-related effect decays as the training budget increases; relative to tuned baselines, the overall strategy effect falls within the prespecified practical-equivalence margin in two of three architectures. A separate grouping-related contrast can persist at long budgets, although its direction and magnitude depend on the architecture.

items.title: FACE: Flow-Guided Angular Channel Estimation Framework for mmWave MIMO Systems
items.author: Samitha Gunarathne, Eslam Eldeeb, Nurul Huda Mahmood, Matti Latva-aho
items.content: Acquiring accurate channel state information (CSI) is essential for millimeter-wave (mmWave) multi-input multi-output (MIMO) systems. However, it remains challenging due to high-dimensional channels, limited pilot observations, and measurement noise. To address these challenges, we propose flow-guided angular channel estimation (FACE), a novel channel estimation framework based on flow matching, an emerging generative modeling paradigm that learns continuous transport dynamics between probability distributions. FACE exploits the inherent angular-domain sparsity of mmWave channels and incorporates the learned flow matching model as a generative channel prior. Numerical results show that FACE consistently achieves higher channel estimation accuracy than both conventional estimators and diffusion-based generative estimator across diverse channel and system configurations. Moreover, FACE maintains high estimation accuracy with fewer pilot observations and achieves an average achievable rate close to the perfect-CSI benchmark. Compared with diffusion-based estimation, FACE requires substantially fewer sampling steps while achieving superior or comparable estimation accuracy, reducing inference time and computational cost. Overall, the proposed framework demonstrates the potential of flow matching for accurate, pilot-efficient, and computationally efficient mmWave MIMO channel estimation.

items.title: Hybrid Quantum Selection of Learning Rates in Language-Model Training: Termination Criteria and an Interaction-Guided Schedule Oracle
items.author: Wei-Che Hung
items.content: Learning-rate choices strongly affect language-model fine-tuning, but the best joint profile across layer groups is generally unknown. This paper studies quantum minimum finding for layer-group learning-rate selection within a hybrid classical-quantum training framework. It combines Durr-Hoyer minimum finding with BBHT search and compares fixed-budget and confidence-based stopping policies using a lookup oracle built from measured profile scores at fixed training checkpoints. The paper then introduces an Interaction-Guided Schedule Oracle that scores and marks joint schedules in superposition without a precomputed score table. Classical one-step loss measurements supply the main, pairwise and three-way interaction effects between layer groups. The circuit adds the effects for each schedule, compares the resulting score with the current baseline score, and marks improving schedules for amplitude amplification. Measured candidates are checked classically before acceptance. Uniform-rate training supplies the initial baseline; using schedules from classical adaptive methods as baselines for joint refinement is left for future work. In closed-loop fine-tuning of a 1.5-billion-parameter language model, each selected schedule drives the next 200 classical training steps. Benchmark accuracies lie within the range observed across five uniform-rate seeds. The results give a working example of how quantum superposition can support adaptive learning-rate selection during training; the remaining quantum limitations are discussed in the paper.

items.title: Disambiguating Moral Circuits and Moral Features in Language Models: Moral content, normative judgment or cue words? Evidence from 14 models
items.author: Davide Liga, Liuwen Yu, Matteo Magnini
items.content: Interpretability methods can locate the attention heads and sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that change the answer a language model gives to a moral prompt, e.g., whether "Stealing medicine for a dying child is morally" continues with "justified" or "wrong". Such a component could respond to moral content, to the judgment of conduct by any norm, or to the word "morally" in the prompt. We built 227 minimal pairs of short phrases, validated by five annotators, whose two versions differ in a moral standard, in another kind of norm (prudence, etiquette, aesthetics or evidence) or in a descriptive quality, and showed them to 14 open-weight models (Llama, Gemma and Qwen, 1B to 14B, base and instruction-tuned), with and without the word "morally". In every model, the heads that change the moral answer belong to an evaluation circuit the models use for every kind of normative judgment we tested: these heads carry the same share of the effect for moral as for other normative pairs (pooled ratio 1.00, 97.5% confidence interval [0.92, 1.07], with the word; 0.90, [0.84, 0.96], without it), and the models need them as much for both. The models need these heads also when nothing in the prompt asks for a judgment, and on 400 scenarios of the ETHICS benchmark, where removing them takes away 37 to 39% of the difference between acceptable and unacceptable scenarios, against 1 to 3% for ten random heads. The SAE features we located respond mostly to the word "morally" rather than to what the phrase is about. The models represent the category of a pair (the standard the annotators assigned to it): it can be read from their hidden states, and, in the eight models we tested, removing the direction that carries it weakens the moral verdict by a few percent, and more than the other verdicts in seven of them. We release the pairs, the ratings, the code, the trained SAE dictionaries and the result files.

items.title: Margin Dynamics for Large Language Model Alignment
items.author: Xingzi Xu, Mehmet Saygin Seyfioglu, Karim Bouyarmane
items.content: Practitioners choose among LLM alignment methods largely by trial and error. We provide a theoretical foundation: each pairwise method defines a vector field on the probability simplex that governs how the model redistributes mass between preferred and dispreferred completions. Projecting onto a single preferred/dispreferred pair reduces this to a one-dimensional margin ODE with a closed-form solution. These solutions reveal that DPO margins grow without bound (logarithmically as $O(\log t)$ in the gradient-flow limit) while IPO margins converge to a finite $1/(2\tau)$; that label noise induces a qualitative phase transition in DPO (unbounded $\to$ bounded) but affects IPO only quantitatively; and that gradient concentration under asymmetric weighting governs trainability at scale. We confirm all three predictions across five model families spanning four benchmarks. The closed-form solutions also enable principled method design: we prove that adding any label smoothing $\varepsilon > 0$ to SimPO creates a finite margin attractor at $\Delta^* = \beta^{-1}\log((1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon)$, while $\varepsilon = 0$ (standard SimPO) has no attractor. We test this across three models (8B-9B) and confirm the prediction: the theory-derived configuration (TPO-S, $\varepsilon = 0.05$) is competitive with the strongest baselines, attaining the highest mean IFEval score among the compared methods on all three, validating that the predicted finite attractor is a usable operating point rather than proposing a new state-of-the-art loss.

items.title: Learning Calibrated and Samplable Predictive Distributions of Surface-Ocean $\Delta p$CO$_2$ Using Tabular Diffusion Models
items.author: Gabriele Accarino, Mohammad M. Amirian, Thea H. Heimdal, Amanda R. Fay, Galen A. McKinley, Viviana Acquaviva
items.content: The ocean absorbs almost 30% of anthropogenic CO$_2$ emissions, but quantifying this sink requires estimating surface-ocean CO$_2$ from observations that are sparse in space and time. Most existing machine-learning estimates of this field are deterministic, giving a single value per grid point, with uncertainty approximated post hoc via residuals, ensembles, or prescribed distributions. We instead learn a conditional predictive distribution for each observation: using Treeffuser, a conditional diffusion model with gradient-boosted-tree score functions, we estimate the full predictive distribution of $\Delta p$CO$_2$ (the sea-air $p$CO$_2$ difference) from 13 environmental, spatial, and temporal predictors. On a held-out SOCAT test set, Treeffuser attains the lowest continuous ranked probability score among the uncertainty-quantification methods evaluated (8.229 $\mu$atm) and the coverage closest to the nominal 68% / 95% levels (0.686 / 0.930), while retaining point-prediction skill comparable to a deterministic XGBoost baseline (RMSE 18.4 vs. 17.7 $\mu$atm; $R^2$ 0.77 vs. 0.79). These results show that conditional diffusion can provide well-calibrated, observation-level uncertainties while largely preserving point-prediction skill. Because Treeffuser is generative, its samples can support probabilistic analyses of $\Delta p$CO$_2$; extending this to spatially coherent field reconstruction will require modeling dependence across grid cells and evaluation on spatially held-out data.

items.title: Regularized Score Centering
items.author: Hao Bai, Chenlu Ye, Xuanchang Zhang, Aviral Kumar, Tong Zhang
items.content: Asynchronous reinforcement learning increases training throughput, but data from stale policies and numerical mismatch between training and inference can destabilize learning. To stabilize off-policy learning, score centering (SC) removes the effect of reward baselines on the expected update. Our gradient diagnostics show less extreme gradients with SC than with importance sampling (IS), but SC can still fail when the learner moves far from the behavior policy that generated the data. To limit this policy mismatch, we introduce Regularized Score Centering (RSC), which adds a reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) penalty to encourage the learner's next-token distribution to stay close to the behavior policy's next-token distribution. RSC works with or without truncated importance sampling (TIS), which caps token importance weights. Our theoretical analysis supports this approach, showing that KL regularization improves convergence guarantees. We evaluate dense and mixture-of-experts models on mathematical reasoning and agentic tasks, including online shopping, tool use, games, and fully asynchronous software engineering. RSC with TIS substantially improves sample efficiency across all agentic benchmarks, attaining higher training rewards with the same number of sampled responses. In final evaluations, it achieves top performance across all six agentic tasks, improving by 14.3% on AppWorld and reaching 9.9 times the strongest baseline's score on BabyAI.

items.title: Chain-of-Thought Controllability Can Reduce Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
items.author: Zheng-Xin Yong, Benjamin Arnav, Miles Wang, Tomek Korbak, Olivia Watkins
items.content: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising tool for detecting hidden goals, off-task behavior, and other failures in AI agents. One risk is that models could deliberately shape their reasoning to make it opaque to monitors. We stress-test this risk through persona-control training: supervised fine-tuning on mathematical reasoning traces rewritten in the voices of diverse personas. This induces a broader ability to control CoT, even though training contains no monitor-evasion examples. In covert side-task evaluations, traces in which a gpt-oss-20b model organism completes the hidden side task contain less monitorable evidence than the base model's. Averaged across evaluations and CoT lengths, weighted by side-task-success counts, the CoT monitorability metric g-mean$^2$ falls from 0.94 for the base model to 0.68 for the model organism without a hiding instruction, and to 0.22 when explicitly instructed to hide. In intervention evaluations, explicit hiding often drives monitorability near zero. The effect extends to a Kimi-K2.6 model organism in agentic environments, though hidden objectives requiring extended reasoning or longer trajectories remain more monitorable than simple single-step side tasks. We further discover that targeted transparency prompts can substantially recover monitorability, sometimes surpassing the base model. These model organisms provide a testbed for studying monitorability failures and potential mitigations. Our code can be found on https://github.com/yongzx/cot-control-model-organism.

items.title: Corrupting Ties: Investigating Robustness to Bias Injection Across Multi-Agent Network Topologies
items.author: Cl\'ea Chataigner, Mina Arzaghi, Florian Carichon, Pablo Piantanida, Golnoosh Farnadi
items.content: AI systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes decision-making contexts, where interactions among components can introduce fairness risks that remain undetected when auditing components or collective outcomes in isolation. As LLM-based multi-agent systems become more prevalent, understanding how biased information propagates through agent interactions is essential for assessing their fairness. We introduce a controlled bias injection framework that replaces selected agent responses with predefined biased ones, enabling an intervention-based analysis of how network topology and injection configurations shape system behavior. We propose decision divergence metrics that quantify the effects of these interventions at the agent, network, and system levels, and evaluate five topologies on three binary classification tasks using LLMs from the Qwen and Gemma families. Sequential networks show the greatest divergence, whereas fully connected and mesh networks show less. Injection position also matters: in star networks, injecting the central agent has larger effects than injecting peripheral agents. Models further differ in whether divergence follows the injected bias. These findings highlight the role of network structure in the propagation of biased information and motivate topology-aware auditing of fairness risks in multi-agent systems.

items.title: A Systematic Survey of Decompilation: Mapping Classical and Machine-Learning Approaches
items.author: Keitaro Shimane, Minami Yoda, Jialong Li, Yutaka Matsuno
items.content: Context: Decompilers reconstruct source-level code from compiled binaries, and analysts rely on them whenever source code is unavailable. Many recent studies apply machine learning (ML), including large language models, to parts of this task. From the primary literature alone, it is unclear where these methods sit in the classical decompilation pipeline and how well their claims are supported. Objectives: We map decompilation research onto a pipeline-centered taxonomy and ask two questions: where classical, ML-trained, and ML-prompted approaches are positioned (RQ1), and how ML-based studies vary in technical design and evaluation evidence (RQ2). Methods: We surveyed 405 decompilation studies from 1973 to 2026, collected through database search and citation tracing. We classified 394 primary studies into eight pipeline stages and two complementary categories. For the 116 ML-based studies that propose or modify decompilation methods, we extracted the model-use strategy, reusable backbones, target platform, and the evidence behind each evaluation. Results: Classical techniques still dominate front-end recovery, IR lifting, and control-flow structuring (277 of 394 primary studies are classical). ML-based work (117 studies) clusters instead around symbol and name recovery, output refinement, and end-to-end translation. Type recovery is the clearest mixed region. Most ML-based studies target native binaries (97 of 116), and most evidence is item-level matching against references (89 of 116); execution-based tests, human or LLM judgment, and downstream-task evidence are much rarer. Conclusion: ML has not displaced the classical pipeline. It has been taken up where a recovered artifact can be posed as a prediction, translation, or refinement problem, and reported gains only make sense when read against the pipeline position and the evidence used to support them.

items.title: Exploring Test Smells Across Programming Languages: A Systematic Mapping Study
items.author: Publio Silva, Carla Bezerra, Ivan Machado, M\'arcio Ribeiro
items.content: Tests are essential for ensuring code quality in software development. However, poor implementation practices can compromise the maintainability and evolution of test code, leading to additional costs and effort. These practices, known as test smells, have been the focus of numerous studies that expanded the catalog of known test smells. Despite this progress, little attention has been given to examining test smells from the perspective of programming languages, particularly their relationship with specific languages or test frameworks. As a result, researchers and practitioners have proposed various approaches and tools to detect and refactor the same test smells across different languages. In this work, we address this gap by analyzing test smells in the literature from a programming language perspective. We conducted a systematic mapping study, gathering data from papers published up to August 2025, examining 117 papers. We identified the most prevalent languages and frameworks associated with test smells, the most common test smells in each language, refactorings for addressing test smells, datasets of test smells, the criticality of specific test smells, and a collection of tools to detect or refactor test smells for various languages and frameworks. Our results show that while many test smells have been addressed, research remains limited to a few languages and frameworks. We also found datasets and detection/refactoring tools for some languages and analyzed the criticality of frequently mentioned test smells. This study highlights the need to expand research to more languages and develop more universal solutions.

items.title: Does Your Agent Need to Know Its Budget? A Placebo-Controlled Experiment on LLM Coding Agents
items.author: Iftesam Nabi, Jarif Ul Alam, Sunzid Hassan, Sabbir Alom Shuvo, Md Faiaz Al Islam, Yead Rahman, Mehrab Hosain
items.content: Organizations deploying autonomous coding agents impose token budgets, yet the causal effects of a budget, and of telling the agent about it, are unmeasured. We conduct a placebo-controlled factorial experiment under a frozen, timestamped protocol, crossing budget enforcement with budget disclosure on two executable program-repair benchmarks (5,835 runs, two open models, three cap levels). Enforcing a calibrated cap reduced task resolution by 20.0 percentage points while reducing tokens per resolved task roughly twelvefold. Disclosing the enforced budget never helped: the placebo-controlled risk difference was -2.8 pp (95% CI [-6.2, +0.7]) at the medium cap and -4.2 pp ([-8.1, -0.2], nominally significant, unadjusted) at the tight cap, with every prompt wording and per-turn feedback variant far below the 10-point effect size of interest. Observed run-to-run outcome variance was roughly 1.5x the uncapped level under caps, though part of this reflects resolution rates moving nearer one half. These results make budget governance for coding agents an enforcement-design problem: no communication variant produced an effect beyond that of an unrelated sentence, which itself raised resolution by 7.2 pp (95% CI [+4.0, +10.5]) over silent enforcement, a sentence effect that only a placebo control removes.

items.title: Wrong yet Confident: Automated Detection of Silent Failures in Location-Dependent Software
items.author: Juan A. Padilla
items.content: We report an experience paper applying round-trip offset---an automated testing oracle for location-dependent software---at deployment scale across 32,019 GPS delivery transactions, corresponding to 24,501 unique coordinates, from a single USDA COVID-19 food assistance deployment in Bayam\'on, Puerto Rico. The oracle tests each geocoder's implicit spatial accuracy claim by measuring the deviation between an input coordinate and the coordinate recovered after reverse-then-forward geocoding, without requiring manual labeling of correctness. We evaluated one community-contributed and two commercial geocoders against this operationally validated corpus. The experience surfaces two distinct failure classes, which we report with their respective denominators because they are not comparable quantities. First, 2,441 of the 24,501 unique coordinates (10.0%) are invisible to all three platforms: an acknowledged failure with no resolution, and a property of the corpus rather than of any one geocoder. Second, and platform-specific: 10.0% of the 13,221 coordinates Google resolves to a civic address exhibit round-trip offsets exceeding 2~km---5.4% of the full corpus---returned with no error signal, against 0.5% for the second commercial platform and 0.04% for the community geocoder. Round-trip offset detects all large-offset failures observed in this dataset while standard resolution-rate evaluation detects none. We document an eight-mode fault taxonomy, a structured comparison of detection methods, and concrete lessons for integrating automated geocoder verification into CI/CD pipelines. The key lesson: resolution rate measures availability; round-trip offset measures correctness. In non-standard addressing environments these two metrics select for opposite behaviors, and only the latter catches the failures that matter for autonomous action.

items.title: Revision-Consistent Code Context for Agents That Edit Their Environment
items.author: Meng Shi
items.content: Editing agents query repositories while simultaneously changing them. Source content, symbols, graph relations, and retrieval state may be maintained by different stores and refreshed at different times. During an update, a successful query can therefore combine facts that never belonged to the same repository state. We call this condition mixed-revision code context. This paper proposes an Agent-visible complete-revision publication contract for composite code-intelligence queries. Before a query-visible publication point, a service must wait, report unavailability, or serve a complete old revision; after that point, it serves the complete new revision. The contract requires a shared version identity and publication boundary across every view returned in one response. We instantiate the method in Codetrip, whose brief operation joins source, symbol, and graph facts. In a controlled comparison on frozen Gin v1.12.0, live-source composition produced two unsafe responses in 150 update trials, whereas complete-revision publication produced none under the same five edit scenarios. We further implement journaled, idempotent publication and terminate the real MCP process at five durable boundaries. All 300 evaluable recovery trials on frozen Gin and Cobra returned complete-new context equivalent to a clean full rebuild, with median restart-to-context latency of 77--131 ms. In a separate rename probe, mixed context occurred in 0/30 Codetrip trials and 30/30 trials for both CodeGraph and codebase-memory-mcp before clean-full-equivalent convergence. The contribution is an Agent-facing safety contract, implementation pattern, and measurement protocol for joining live repository bytes with asynchronously derived facts. Every successful composite response consequently has a testable repository-state meaning, including after interruption.

items.title: A Chain-of-Thought Prompt Engineering Framework for Automated Technical Specification Generation in Enterprise Integration: A Real-World Case Study
items.author: Aryan Dhingra, Gokul Menon, Anusha Antony
items.content: Technical Specification Documents (TSDs) translate functional requirements into implementable designs and are mandatory artifacts in governed Enterprise Application Integration (EAI) programs, yet their production remains a manual, expertise-intensive bottleneck. Large Language Models (LLMs) have been studied extensively for code generation, but long-form, template-governed engineering documents remain comparatively unexplored. This paper reports an industrial case study, conducted during a migration of more than 250 enterprise integrations to Microsoft Azure Integration Services at a large Australian wholesale distributor, that introduces a chain-of-thought prompt-engineering framework for automated TSD generation using GitHub Copilot. The framework combines a two-phase generation architecture that grounds the model in the functional specification, organizational standards, and the approved template; a six-stage prompting pipeline with human validation checkpoints; and Prompt-as-a-Code, under which prompts are version-controlled and reviewed as engineering artifacts. Applied to a stratified sample of fifteen production interfaces, the framework reduced TSD authoring effort from 793 to 300 person-hours, a 62.2% pooled reduction and a 64.0% mean per-document reduction (Wilcoxon signed-rank, n = 15, p < 0.001), at 74.3% reviewer-assessed accuracy and 3.7/5 developer satisfaction. Benefits degrade monotonically with interface complexity: between the simplest and most complex bands, effort reduction falls from 70.6% to 58.9% and accuracy from 91% to 62.5%, and the residual human effort concentrates in diagrams, sequence flows, and cross-system integration content. We additionally report comparative observations of GPT-4.1/5 and Claude Sonnet 4, as well as Copilot's Ask and Agent interaction modes, offering reusable, practice-grounded guidance for enterprise settings.

items.title: The Defense Rests: A Courtroom-Inspired Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Automated Safety Case Generation
items.author: Gerhard Yu (Alex), Amanuel Aknaw (Alex), Amir Ali Mohaghegh (Alex), Yong Song (Alex), Cao, Alvine B. Belle
items.content: Safety cases are widely used to demonstrate that mission-critical systems, such as autonomous vehicles and unmanned aerial systems, can operate safely after deployment. However, manually constructing safety cases is complex, time-consuming, and labor-intensive, which calls for the proposal of automated approaches to support their creation. Inspired by the legal nature of safety case construction, we formalize the safety case creation problem through a courtroom analogy, where stakeholders collaboratively propose, examine, criticize, review, improve and validate safety claims and their supporting evidence. In this analogy, the safety analyst acts as a prosecutor by identifying hazards and safety concerns, while the assurance case developer serves as a defense attorney by constructing and substantiating safety arguments. An orchestrator acts as a judge by coordinating stakeholder interactions, and a review board serves as a jury by assessing argument completeness and persuasiveness. Based on this formalization, we propose eTrustWare, a Large Language Model (LLM)-based multi-agent framework for automated safety case generation and review. Our experiments on several safety cases of ML-enabled autonomous driving systems demonstrate the feasibility of coordinated LLM-based agents for generating safety cases.

items.title: Stochastic Modeling of the Mean Time Between Software Failures: A review
items.author: Gabriel Pena, Veronica Moreno, Nestor Barraza
items.content: A review of several models for the software failure detection stochastic process is per- formed. We focus on how the Mean Time Between Failures is obtained from those models and present a comparative study. The models considered involve some of the well known based on non- homogeneous Poisson processes and a recently proposed model based on contagion. Our main target is to evaluate the models performance when they are applied to modern software projects developed under Agile methodologies. Recently developed Software Engineering practices (TDD, Scrum, etc.), propose an iterative procedure be- tween development, testing and debugging, introducing this way, particular challenges to Software Reliability modeling. As opposed to the non-homogeneous Poisson processes, the failure rate of the contagion model depends not just on time but also on the number of previously detected failures. All the considered models are particular cases of non- homogeneous Birth Processes, a general fundamental theory on how to obtain time to failure and time between failures expectations is also shown.

items.title: From AIOps Pipelines to Agentic Service Operations: A Survey of Capability, Authority, and Evidence
items.author: Hailiang Zhao, Wenzhuo Qian, Jianwei Yin, Shuiguang Deng
items.content: Modern service systems combine rapidly changing dependencies, heterogeneous telemetry, and operational actions whose side effects may amplify an incident. Conventional AIOps research has produced effective detectors, localizers, and diagnostic models, yet surveys typically organize them by task, telemetry modality, or learning technique. Such taxonomies describe what a method predicts, but not which decisions it may make or which evidence justifies that authority. We survey the transition from AIOps pipelines to agentic service operations through three coupled lenses: capability, operational authority, and evaluation evidence. We first relate SOA, microservices, Kubernetes, service meshes, and serverless platforms to the incident lifecycle. We then review conventional AIOps methods and audit 22 language-model-enabled systems according to their evaluated behavior rather than their intended autonomy. The audit shows that most systems remain copilots or read-only investigators. Only two exercise write authority; both use constrained action envelopes, and neither carries controlled production-outcome evidence. Building on these findings, we synthesize a four-plane reference architecture, evidence grades, an evaluation ladder, and a controlled adoption path. Together, these artifacts clarify which claims current evaluations support and what evidence is still required for dependable agentic service operations.

items.title: On Improving the Adoption, Usability, and Retention of Static Application Security Testing (SAST) Tools
items.author: Zachary Douglas Wadhams
items.content: As the Internet connects more of the world, software vulnerabilities create growing security risks. Because software developers are responsible for building and maintaining secure applications, they rely on tools and techniques that help identify vulnerabilities early in development. Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tools analyze source code to identify potential security weaknesses before software is deployed. Although SAST can help developers address vulnerabilities proactively, these tools also present usability and adoption challenges. This thesis examines those challenges and explores ways to improve the adoption, usability, and continued use of SAST. First, a literature review of 89 research works related to SAST implementation and continued usage identifies recurring developer concerns, including false positives and other usability barriers that can reduce trust in SAST results. Second, the thesis presents a process for automating the execution of SAST tools and formatting their output so that findings are more meaningful and actionable to developers. A real-world use case evaluates an implementation of this process and gathers developer feedback. Participants reported satisfaction with several aspects of the process and indicated that it increased their willingness to use the SAST tool.

items.title: The Software Engineering Factory: Engineering Accountability and Control in the Age of Abundant Code
items.author: Ahmed E. Hassan, Zhe Chen, Amr E. Mohamed, Keheliya Gallaba, Daniel German, Waleed Kadous, Gustavo A. Oliva, Radin Shayanfar, Paul Stack, Haoxiang Zhang
items.content: AI agents can now plan, write, test, review, and revise code at a volume no human organization can inspect line by line. Final code review therefore cannot remain the primary organizational control for owning code changes. The Software Engineering (SE) Factory moves control into the process that produces the code. The Factory protocols define how work moves, what evidence must exist before it can proceed, and who owns the result. A deterministic protocol engine, implemented in conventional code rather than prompts, enforces those protocols by controlling stage transitions, requiring evidence, and invoking gates and human escalation, where needed, before work can advance. The SE Factory preserves human authority over consequential decisions and makes accountable acceptance possible without requiring humans to supervise every agent action. The SE Factory is not a dark factory. Humans remain in control by defining the scope and granularity of delegation, the boundaries and escalation conditions, and the consequential decisions that require accountable human judgment. We draw on our experience building three distinct SE Factory implementations, all of which have undergone multiple iterations and two of which are publicly available as open-source systems, into ten principles for conceiving, building, and operating SE Factories at scale, grounded in the organizational and technical realities of our implementations. We do not claim that these principles are exhaustive or constitute the only viable foundation for an SE Factory. Rather, we offer them as a conceptual scaffold and shared vocabulary for reasoning about SE Factories, evaluating their designs, and guiding their evolution. Our goal is to catalyze a community-wide dialogue that moves software engineering beyond controls designed for human-scale code production toward a disciplined, scalable, and trustworthy agentic future.

items.title: Trustworthy AI Teammates for Software Engineering: A Research Agenda for Lifecycle Context, Explainability, and Agentic Collaboration
items.author: Glaucia Melo
items.content: Large Language Models are rapidly changing software engineering (SE) practice by supporting code generation, testing, debugging, documentation, and program comprehension. Yet most current AI coding assistants remain reactive tools: they respond to local prompts, rely on limited context, and provide suggestions whose rationale is often difficult for developers to inspect. This paper argues that the next phase of AI-assisted SE requires a shift from coding assistants to trustworthy AI teammates. We present a research agenda for human-AI co-evolution in SE, organized around three requirements. First, AI systems must become lifecycle-aware, reasoning across requirements and other deployment artifacts rather than isolated files or prompts. Second, they must provide principled explanations that expose assumptions, evidence, trade-offs, and risks in ways that support developer judgment. Third, they must enable agentic collaboration, in which specialized AI agents participate in software workflows while preserving human oversight and accountability. We propose an evaluation framework that moves beyond isolated functional correctness toward collaborative quality, including contextual alignment, trust calibration, maintenance recovery cost, and traceability. We conclude by outlining open challenges for designing AI systems that improve software quality without weakening human understanding, agency, or responsibility.

items.title: Evaluating AST-Derived Knowledge Graph Retrieval for AIOps Incident Diagnosis in Apache Kafka
items.author: Shashank Mishra, Shweta Mishra
items.content: Incident diagnosis requires retrieving source-linked operational evidence from large codebases. We evaluate graph-augmented retrieval for Apache Kafka using an abstract-syntax-tree (AST)-derived ownership graph over 1,600 source-linked log records and an audited benchmark of 315 incident-style queries covering 103 unique targets. Vector-only retrieval is a strong baseline at Recall@20 of 0.956, and neither static nor confidence-guided staged AST expansion significantly improves Recall@20 over it. As an external control we evaluate HippoRAG, a published text-derived graph-retrieval system, against its own ColBERTv2 retrieval backbone. Against ColBERTv2-only (Recall@20 0.803), HippoRAG attained 0.308; a post-hoc document-ensemble sensitivity raised Recall@20 to 0.648 but did not eliminate the deficit. Relative to static expansion, staging reduces cross-encoder pair workload and measured reranking time by about 52%. A manually evaluated 100-query downstream study finds no significant root-cause-correctness advantage for AST-derived structural evidence.

items.title: X-LocVul: An Evidence-Propagation Audit of Cascaded C/C++ Vulnerability Detection, Localization, and Explanation
items.author: Hoang-Phuong-Linh Le, Quyet-Thang Huynh
items.content: Developer-facing vulnerability analysis should link a function-level warning to a source location and a supported explanation. Cascaded systems can propagate weak evidence despite plausible components. We present X-LocVul, a measurement-first audit of a modular C/C++ detector-localizer-explainer pipeline combining UniXCoder, CodeT5, and Qwen2.5-Coder. We test whether evidence passed across stages is useful, merely source-resident, or misleading. Under duplication and temporal-leakage controls, UniXCoder has higher point estimates than CodeBERT, but true-CWE supervision is statistically indistinguishable from a shuffled-CWE control on PR-AUC, MCC, and vulnerable-class F1. Raw generated statements fail exact source matching in 90.83% of cases. Fuzzy projection reaches 83.79% Top-1 accuracy and exceeds semantic projection by 1.59 percentage points, although its advantage over raw ranking is not established. In a randomized, condition-label-masked two-rater evaluation of 50 paired cases, a predicted line improves evidence support, whereas a predicted CWE improves no endpoint. Oracle evidence improves evidence support (Holm-adjusted p=0.00453) and CWE consistency (p=3.49 x 10^-7), but not root-cause quality after correction (p=0.250); unsupported claims remain common. A chronological stress test retains ranking signal (ROC-AUC 0.782; PR-AUC 0.110), while the transferred threshold yields zero recall and F1. The contribution is not a state-of-the-art claim, but an auditable account of evidence construction, transfer, and consumption. It separates source residency from localization correctness, auxiliary labels from semantic supervision, and predicted evidence from useful evidence. Public E4 scores regenerate all 15 tests; missing manifests, final prompts, and profiler logs bound stronger reproducibility claims.

items.title: Usage Patterns of Programming Languages and Tools: A Systematic Literature Review
items.author: Sherlock A. Licorish, Natalie Grattan
items.content: Technology and the popularity of languages and tools are rapidly evolving. Thus, it is important to constantly assess the most popular languages and tools used in industry, furthering the collaboration between research and the software industry. In this study, we use a systematic literature review and investigate 37 studies published between 2015 -- 2024, which explored the programming languages, IDEs and CI tools used in industry. We observed that Java is most often listed among the most popular languages, and there are limited studies that investigate specific IDE usage. Also, Travis CI and GitHub Actions are the most common CI tools identified as being top CI tools used in industry. Overall, evidence shows that there is a lack of research focused on popular languages and tools used in industry, largely as there are many limitations with the possible methodology approaches. For example, lack of access to closed-source projects and sampling biases are potential issues that limit our understanding of popular languages and tools used in industry. In this regard, there is a need for more recent studies into development tools used in industry, involving multiple research approaches, to balance the limitations of each approach.

items.title: Reusing Battle-tested Code: A Systematic Literature Review of Automated Software Transplantation
items.author: Thanatad Songpetchmongkol, Earl T. Barr, Mark Harman, Federica Sarro, Justyna Petke
items.content: Software reuse remains a fundamental challenge in software engineering, often caught between the security risks of external libraries and the reliability concerns of generative AI. Automated software transplantation offers a compelling alternative by enabling the direct extraction and integration, into new host systems, of battle-tested logic (code that has already survived the rigors of production, possibly over many years of extensive in-production use). This paper presents a systematic literature review to evaluate the current state-of-the-art and identify the remaining barriers preventing this technology from becoming a mainstream engineering practice. We identified 27 distinct automated software transplantation approaches. Our analysis reveals that while the adaptation of code is highly automated, significant bottlenecks remain in the manual prerequisite steps of organ location and test suite augmentation. We conclude with a research roadmap that suggests how these manual obstacles might be overcome, including the strategic use of Large Language Models to assist in identifying and verifying high-value, production-hardened logic for transplantation.

items.title: A Model-Driven Automation Pipeline for Building Operation
items.author: Elias Kohler, Sascha Hammes, Michael Vierhauser, Philipp Zech
items.content: Building Control Systems (BCS) engineering in the Architecture, Engineering, Construction & Operations (AECO) domain remains a complex, manual, and error-prone process, with fractured tools and manual commissioning causing design and built reality to diverge into a performance gap. We argue that a fully integrated and automated, tool-supported workflow spanning design, programming, and operation is feasible and can improve efficiency while reducing manual effort and configuration errors. Building on model-driven engineering, we present an automated process pipeline for modeling, programming, and auto-commissioning BCS. It uses two domain-specific modeling languages with tooling support to synthesize and deploy executable artifacts from platform-independent models, replacing a fractured, multi-stakeholder handoff process with a defined four-step workflow and improving consistency across the engineering lifecycle. Our evaluation reports notable efficiency gains, improved adaptability, moderate-to-high user acceptance, and good performance with solid scalability.

items.title: Fragmented Markers, Mixed Results: A Systematic Review of AI Coding Assistants and Developer Productivity
items.author: Annemarie Wittig, Alina Mailach, Norbert Siegmund
items.content: AI coding assistants are increasingly embedded in software engineering practice, yet the literature still offers no cumulative, easily interpretable picture of their effects on software developer productivity. The central problem is not a lack of studies, but a lack of comparability: prior work operationalizes productivity through heterogeneous markers, settings, and reporting styles, making cross-study conclusions difficult. To address this, we conduct a staged systematic literature review. In the first stage, we synthesize studies that explicitly examine developer productivity. In the second, we extend the scope to productivity-related developer outcomes using SPACE as a theory-informed lens, capturing human-centered evidence that explicit productivity studies often omit. Across both stages, we analyze how productivity is operationalized, which confounding factors are discussed, and how reported effects are distributed. We identify 187 unique productivity and productivity-related markers, while individual studies typically only use five, revealing a broad but highly fragmented evidence base. Explicit productivity research is dominated by time-, output-, and artifact-oriented proxies, whereas the broader SPACE-aligned corpus makes satisfaction, psychological aspects, and well-being substantially more visible. Reported effects are often positive, but this pattern is stronger in perceived and tendency-based findings than in objective or statistically evaluated ones. Overall, the literature suggests that AI coding assistants can support productivity, but current evidence does not yet support simple, context-independent conclusions. The key contribution of this review is therefore a structured basis for making productivity evidence more interpretable, multidimensional, and comparable across studies.

items.title: Measuring Human-AI Alignment as an Early Indicator for Effective Collaboration in Hybrid SE Teams
items.author: Andreas Metzger
items.content: As AI agents increasingly integrate into software engineering (SE) processes, ensuring effective collaboration in these hybrid teams becomes a critical challenge. While existing metrics focus on observing dynamic run-time performance, there is a lack of systematic, static measurements for early human-AI alignment -- the degree to which an AI's actions and granularity map to human expectations. This position paper proposes a research agenda to develop an SE-specific alignment metric suite drawing principles from software architecture, organizational psychology, and human-computer interaction. Furthermore, it outlines a validation methodology using concepts and techniques from business process monitoring (BPM) and introduces static assessment tools leveraging declarative BPM languages to ensure agents adhere to specific project constraints.

items.title: Trusting Trust in AI Software Engineering Agents: The Why, What, and How?
items.author: Pranav V, Sridhar Chimalakonda, Vibhu Saujanya Sharma, Vikrant Kaulgud
items.content: AI software engineering agents are increasingly integrated into development workflows, from autocomplete assistants to autonomous repair agents and multi-agent software development pipelines. Trust matters because these agents can produce, revise, and pass on artifacts that developers, other agents, or organisations may later rely on under uncertainty and risk. Yet trust in such systems is often treated as a single measurable property of an AI system. This is insufficient for software engineering, where trust depends on who relies on the agent, how that reliance is structured, and which properties must hold in that deployment. We propose a structural framework for reasoning about trust in AI software engineering agents. Inspired by the recursive nature of trust in software systems, we decompose trust into three analytical questions: Why trust?, identifying the trust scenario; What trust?, identifying the trust configuration; and How much trust?, identifying the trust properties. From these questions, we derive three scenarios, four configurations, and five trust-relevant properties, state which of these are closed by construction and which remain open to revision, and instantiate the resulting profile on a ChatDev-style multi-agent workflow. The framework is conceptual, and is offered as a foundation for the empirical work that would validate it, rather than as a numerical trust metric.

items.title: We Fixed the Scorer First, and Cluster Correction Killed Our Own Planted-Defect Result in AI Code Review
items.author: Sungjin Kwon
items.content: Judging an AI code-review pipeline only by how much it catches hides an axis: what it dropped. Stronger selection raises precision for free; the cost never reaches the report. We ran four arms on the same eight cases, one scorer, asking whether planted-defect detection can rise without raising the claim error rate. Three repetitions are nested in eight cases, so p is reported per contrast and twice: under an exact permutation test over cases (2^8 arrangements) the two contrasts publishable under independence (Fisher p=0.017, 0.019) move to 0.0625 and 0.109, and after Holm correction no contrast separates. This is "not observable with this design," not "no effect": the sign test needs six discordant cases in one direction, its realized type-I rate under the null is 0.0078, and 80% power needs a per-case win probability near 0.80; closing it takes 12-25 cases, not repetitions. Within a run, a second pass never removes what the first found (0/24, 0/24 paired losses) while its gains (+3, +2) fall in one case; baselines on byte-identical prompts differed 15/24 vs 20/24, so run-to-run variance exceeds the effect. The claim error rate is 0.0% (0/178), with no upper bound on the rate claimed; scorer discrimination was measured with pre-registered positive controls (12/12 fabricated claims rejected, 0 false rejections). We retract our original causal explanation and report the instrument defects we hit. The contributions are not the numbers: (1) fixing the instrument before seeing results, then killing our own main effect with it; (2) the identity eps-hat = eps-hat(pi): a reported error rate is computed only on the subset a retention policy kept, silent about what was dropped, so it does not identify the quantity an irreversible gate needs; no improvement in the number promotes an automated verdict to publish, delete, or history-rewrite surfaces; a mechanized refusal enforces this.

items.title: A Survey of Modeling Languages for Automotive Digital Twins
items.author: Jer\^om\'e Pfeiffer, Dominik Fuch{\ss}, Thomas K\"uhn, Dirk Neumann, Christer Neim\"ock, Anne Koziolek, Andreas Wortmann
items.content: The demand for digital twins and suitable modeling techniques in the automotive industry is increasing rapidly. Yet, there is no common understanding of digital twins in automotive, nor are there modeling techniques established to create automotive digital twins. Recent studies on digital twins focus on the analysis of the literature on digital twins for automotive or in general and, thus, neglect the industrial perspective of automotive practitioners. To mitigate this gap between scientific literature and the industrial perspective, we conducted a questionnaire survey among experts in the German automotive industry to identify (i) the desired purposes for and capabilities of digital twins, (ii) the modeling techniques related to engineering and operating digital twins across the phases of automotive development, and (iii) the role informal models play during automotive development. To this end, we contacted 189 members of the Software-Defined Car research project and received 96 responses. The results show that digital twins are considered most useful in the usage and support phase of automotive development, representing vehicles as-operated. Moreover, simulation models, source code, and business process models are currently considered the most important models to be integrated into a digital twin alongside the associated, established tools. Furthermore, informal models are frequently created digitally, e.g., using PowerPoint, mainly employed for communication and documentation during the conception and development phase.

items.title: A Critical Appraisal and Motivated Intruder Test of A Search Dataset Anonymised for the Purposes of the EU Digital Markets Act
items.author: Ghislain d'Entremont, Lisa Pilgram, Sophie Stalla-Bourdillon, Renee Gil, Lucy Mosquera, Olga Vovk, Khaled El Emam
items.content: This study evaluated the European Commission's anonymisation measures for Alphabet's search-data sharing under Article 6(11) of the Digital Markets Act against European Data Protection Board guidance and contemporary practice, and assessed re-identification through motivated intruder testing. The measures focus on search end-users, leaving other individuals mentioned in queries insufficiently protected, and do not explicitly address inference. The accompanying controls and safeguards reflect good practice for managing residual risk. Motivated intruder testing targeted 98,501 individuals across six countries using publicly available profiles. Google-verified matches yielded a re-identification rate of 0.094%, below the study's 0.47% per-team threshold. Each verified match required about three hours (Euro 105), excluding Google verification and Gemini costs, suggesting limited cost deterrence. All country-level rates were below the threshold, but one region exceeded it. The threshold drew on conservative precedents, adjusted for data quality, verification, controls and safeguards, assuming five independent attack teams. Some sensitivity scenarios exceeded the threshold, but relied on strong assumptions, such as treating all uncertain matches as correct. Results may not generalise beyond the targeted population, and ethics requirements constrained the attacks. Personal data detection recall was assumed rather than tested: the minimum defensible recall was 0.88, with 0.976 recommended. However, missed identifiers outside the allow-list would remain in the dataset. Under the study's contextual framework, assumptions and testing limitations, identity-disclosure risk was considered insignificant. This finding does not resolve the gaps concerning inference and other individuals' information; safeguards remain necessary.

items.title: Stop Early, Stay Simple: Evidence Acquisition for Power System Fault and Attack Diagnosis
items.author: S M Zia Ur Rashid, Sazidul Islam Hira, Rupesh Sah, Suman Rath
items.content: Diagnostic models for cyber-physical power systems usually inspect every telemetry source for every event, although some events are clear from one source and others need several. We ask when a learned policy for choosing that evidence is worth its added complexity. To answer this, we present ActiGrid, a benchmark framework for active evidence acquisition that pairs a classifier trained to tolerate missing modalities with a Double Deep Q-Network (DQN), which either requests another source or stops and diagnoses but never operates grid actuators. On the public TU Delft digital substation and MSU/ORNL power system attack benchmarks, we compare the DQN with fixed subsets and orders, calibrated entropy stopping, a greedy value of information rule, and tree ensembles trained per subset. The learned policy does adapt to what it observes, yet it is statistically indistinguishable from entropy stopping on TU Delft and Pareto dominated by simple controls on MSU/ORNL, while compact subset classifiers outperform it while reading fewer sources on both benchmarks. Entropy stopping run over those subset classifiers reaches the highest mean Macro-F1 on TU Delft (0.928 while reading 57% of the sources) but brings no saving over a static three source subset on MSU/ORNL, where no method exceeds 0.45 Macro-F1. Selective acquisition can pay off, but on these benchmarks it does not need a learned policy.

items.title: Watermark Evidence under Open-Weight LLM Modification: Exact Bounds for Low-Rank Output Watermarks
items.author: Prashant Shekhar, Dumindu Samaraweera, Caroline Howard
items.content: Open-weight language models can continue generating after their released weights are modified, while a watermark verifier still scores outputs against the original base and marked models. We study how such modifications change the evidence available to an OpenStamp-style verifier. At each shared prefix, we represent the modification as a residual in the next-token logits. We derive an exact finite-vocabulary lower bound on the expected log-likelihood-ratio evidence under a residual-span constraint, along with a sharp span-only deviation bound. We also characterize the first-order evidence shift through a covariance term with an explicit second-order remainder, and determine the residual span needed to reach a target evidence level. For sequence-level detection, we derive an exact conditional exponential-moment bound and combine it with a supermartingale argument and a distribution-free order-statistic tolerance bound. This yields a high-confidence upper bound on miss probability after attack selection on calibration data and evaluation on independent certification continuations. In experiments with OpenStamp on Llama-2-7B and Mistral-7B-v0.3, INT8 quantization and 30% pruning retain test true-positive rates of 85.6-94.8%, while 500-step LoRA fine-tuning lowers them to 28.8% and 11.6%. The covariance prediction tracks the measured mean LoRA evidence drift on both models, with no remainder-bound violations across 160,000 test prefixes. Additionally, we observe zero false positives among 500 base-model continuations per model. Through these theoretical and empirical results, the current research provides a better understanding of watermark robustness to model-editing/tuning attacks.

items.title: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Ars Technica review
items.author: Kyle Orland
items.content: Just a minute ago, I was shooting my way out of a cocaine deal gone wrong, darting behind furniture for cover. Now I’m sitting on the floor of my home, working through the instructions to construct an Ikea-style coffee table with my partner. A tiny heart with a plus sign pops up, showing that our relationship is stronger for this quotidian domestic effort. This is the contrast at the heart of Grand Theft Auto VI, a game that seems to revel in both action movie bombast and the mundanities of everyday life for an up-and-coming young criminal couple. The reimagined and expanded Vice City is still the grand, crude, satirical criminal playground you’d expect after 25 years of 3D Grand Theft Auto games. And that world is as full, detailed, technically impressive, and polished as you would expect after this latest installment received a reported billion-dollar budget and roughly a decade of development work involving thousands of Rockstar staffers. items.title: Sector Snapshot: Investors Turn Up The Volume On Voice AI
items.author: Judy Rider
items.content: Voice AI — technology that lets computers understand and generate human speech — is drawing billions of dollars from investors as startups find more ways to put it to work. Companies developing or offering the technology have raised at least $9.5 billion in venture funding so far in 2026, according to Crunchbase data. The recipients range from companies building speech recognition and generation tools to those offering voice agents for customer service. Others use voice AI for creative work or accessibility, or build the infrastructure and chips that power the technology. The broad trend: Investors are putting more money into fewer startups developing or offering voice AI technology and are backing everything from automated customer service to speech generation and content creation. The funding surge also reflects the broader AI boom, with some of the largest rounds going to infrastructure and generative media companies whose businesses extend beyond voice. Multiple companies are raising rounds in quick succession. The numbers: So far in 2026, startups developing or offering voice AI technology have raised $9.5 billion globally, Crunchbase data shows. As of Nov. 11, funding had already exceeded 2025 by 67%, with 154 reported deals versus 273 in 2025. Overall, deal volume is on track to fall for a second consecutive year — pointing to a market where investors are putting more money into fewer companies. Unsurprisingly, given the AI boom, funding for the space has continued to climb in recent years compared to past levels, surging from $2.8 billion in 2021 to $5.7 billion in 2025. Notable rounds The largest rounds in Crunchbase’s voice AI micro-industry went well beyond speech synthesis, encompassing infrastructure, generative media and customer service agents. The biggest individual financing went to Fireworks AI, which raised a $1.5 billion Series D in July at a $17.5 billion valuation. The San Mateo, California-based company is an AI infrastructure provider whose offerings include speech recognition. Atreides Management, Index Ventures and TCV co-led the round, with participation from investors including Nvidia and Lightspeed Venture Partners. San Francisco-based Fal was the largest funding recipient across multiple rounds in 2026, raising $1.65 billion in total. That included a $1.3 billion Series F led by Bessemer Venture Partners, completed in October at a reported $16 billion valuation, doubling its valuation from its $350 million Sequoia Capital-led financing in April. The company provides infrastructure for running image, video and audio models. Customer service AI also attracted substantial investment. San Francisco-based Sierra raised $950 million in May, led by Tiger Global and GV, at a reported $15.8 billion valuation. Its platform lets businesses deploy agents across voice, chat and other customer channels. Meanwhile, Amsterdam-based Wonderful raised a $550 million Series C in September, led by Insight Partners, at a $5 billion valuation. That followed a $150 million Series B in March, bringing its total 2026 funding to $700 million as it expanded from conversational agents into broader enterprise automation. Among companies focused on AI-generated speech, New York-based ElevenLabs announced a $500 million Series D in February, led by Sequoia Capital, at an $11 billion valuation. That was more than triple its valuation a year earlier. Additional institutional and strategic investors joined in later tranches, bringing the Series D total to $561 million. ElevenLabs allows creators, enterprises and others to use AI software to replicate voices in dozens of languages. The company is investing in conversational agents, expressive speech and dubbing. Beijing-based ModelBest, which develops compact AI models that run on devices, also ranks among the largest recipients of funding this year, with a $591 million Series C in July. Exits Voice AI companies have also begun delivering exits. In January, Deepgram acquired OfOne, which automates restaurant and drive-thru orders. In September, Inworld acquired Ultravox, a developer of conversational voice AI technology. The sector also saw an IPO. Neosapience, the South Korean company behind synthetic voice platform Typecast, listed on the KOSDAQ on Sept. 21. Looking ahead, additional acquisitions are in the pipeline. Automation Anywhere agreed to acquire Boost.ai, an enterprise voice and chat AI provider, in October. And Deepgram announced plans to acquire Daily, creator of the Pipecat voice-agent framework. More recently, Five9 agreed to acquire Level AI for $325 million in cash, adding technology that analyzes customer conversations, assists contact-center workers and automates voice and digital interactions. The Level AI transaction is expected to close by year’s end. Overall, the space is booming, and it doesn’t look like interest in voice AI will die anytime soon. Tom Hulme, managing partner and head of Europe at GV, told Crunchbase News in 2025 that one of the most exciting trends he believes is underway in the growth of voice AI is that “we’re returning to humanity’s most natural form of communication.” After decades of adapting ourselves to technology, “technology is finally adapting to us,” he said.
