items.title: What To Measure When ARR Isn’t Enough
items.author: Guest Author
items.content: By Kenza Zayani In October, reports that OpenAI‘s annualized revenue was running well below earlier estimates sent AI-linked stocks sharply lower and prompted a fresh round of scrutiny over AI valuations. It also reopened a question investors have been circling for a while: Is ARR still the right way to describe an AI business? The limitations have been understood for some time. ARR was built for software companies selling predictable annual contracts, which is only part of how most AI companies make money. Through the early part of the generative AI boom, growth was steep enough that few people pressed the point. The OpenAI episode has made it harder to leave alone, partly because it showed how much weight public markets now place on a single private company’s numbers. For founders, this is worth paying attention to now rather than later. A cohort of AI companies is reaching the growth-capital stage, and the questions they face in diligence are changing. What ARR was built for Kenza Zayani of RTP Global. ARR became standard in the mid- to late-2000s, when software moved from licence fees to recurring subscriptions. A customer signed for 12 months, revenue became predictable and annualizing it was arithmetic rather than forecasting. The first generation of post-ChatGPT companies inherited it without much examination, despite earning money in a different way. Most now run hybrid models: a subscription base with consumption charges on top, billed against API calls, tokens processed or compute used. A growing number charge per outcome. An annualized figure blends revenue a customer has committed to with revenue that depends on what they use next month. What gets presented as ARR is usually a revenue run rate: recent revenue multiplied out to an annual figure. That is a reasonable way to describe momentum, and a less reliable guide to the year ahead. The first question an investor tends to ask is what the figure actually counts. Companies that sell partly through partners can report either the full value of those sales or only the share they keep, and the two conventions produce very different numbers for the same business. Both are legitimate, but the two are not necessarily comparable. Take two companies both reporting a $10 million annualized run rate. In the first, most of that revenue is contracted, and comes from customers whose usage has expanded steadily over 12 months. In the second, it rests on a handful of customers whose consumption spiked in the last quarter. These are not similar businesses. The first has demonstrated that customers keep coming back and spending more. Nothing in the headline figure tells you that. Looking beyond the headline If a single figure cannot separate those two businesses, the question is what can. The answer depends on the stage. At pre-seed and seed, the number matters. A steep trajectory can point to market demand, to customers willing to pay, and to a team beginning to crack go-to-market. A run rate isn’t generally expected to predict the year at that size. Later you need more. What matters is the revenue behind the number: customer concentration, how much is contracted rather than consumed, how predictable that revenue is, and whether the gross margins hold as volume rises. Retention and expansion are the centerpiece. They tell you how essential a product has become and whether it will still be in use in a few years. Churn is diagnostic in a way a growth figure never is. It can point to demand the product is not answering, pricing that does not match the value, a need that was never really recurring, or a market shallower than it first looked. What investors will expect next ARR has been a staple of how high-growth tech companies demonstrate momentum for such a long time that it’s not likely to disappear anytime soon. What is changing is how much weight that single number can carry on its own. Expect more investors to ask what a figure actually counts, how much of it is committed revenue, and what retention looks like by cohort. The founders who have those answers ready will tell a much more convincing story than a single number ever could. Kenza Zayani is an early-stage investor at RTP Global, based in London. She is drawn to ambitious founders tackling the most challenging problems, with a particular interest in AI from infrastructure to applications. Zayani has built experience in venture capital across stages, and at RTP Global, she brings her multistage experience and data-driven approach to company building with founders. items.title: How The Verge is picking which Black Friday deals to share
items.author: Cameron Faulkner
items.content: For the past month, we’ve been inundated with Black Friday deals, signaling what’s to come on the biggest shopping day of the year in the US. We routinely get dozens of press releases a day, coming from brands big and small that hope that we’ll publicize these offers. Of course, the companies would prefer that we don’t do any research on these deals to see if they’re actually good, and most don’t provide any of the necessary context we’re looking for when vetting them. Most indicators of a good deal are confusing — not just for us, but for anyone who’s shopping. Groundwork Collaborative recently published its findings about the unclear manner in which Amazon displays deals. Its researchers tracked a selection of products ahead of Black Friday and Cyber Monday in 2024 and 2025, and they claim that nearly one in three products advertised as deals on Amazon didn’t offer savings during the actual shopping events. The investigation also found that nearly a tenth of the deals it examined were more expensive during the sales events than on some days in the month leading up to them. Something we commonly see on Amazon and attempt to correct for in our coverage are good deals with inflated discount claims. As in, the original retail amount (the “list” price) is sometimes higher than the usual day-to-day price to make the savings seem more substantial. Sometimes, the manufacturer’s suggested retail price (MSRP) is what’s shown, though that’s not always the case. In a recent statement to investigative journalist Ronan Farrow, an unattributed Amazon spokesperson shared that its “List Price” can also be aggregated from the past 90 to 180 days of prices, not the past 30 days as Groundwork Collaborative’s research states, and is based on prices from Amazon itself and other competing retailers. However, in our experience, the confusing way pricing and discounts are communicated isn’t limited to Amazon. View this post on Instagram The group’s findings show how easy it is to distrust the prices you see, especially online, where dynamic pricing sometimes comes into play. Regardless of retailer practices, we understand the importance of curating what you see on The Verge with care. Vetting deals for coverage consideration is a big, albeit invisible, part of our jobs, even outside of big shopping events. Most of what we’re pitched day to day, or what we see in our respective feeds, never hits the site because it doesn’t meet our standards. Even when the deal is for a product we’ve tested and really enjoy — our north star for what to cover on the deals front — that alone doesn’t guarantee coverage. We often skip covering deals that aren’t as good as a retailer or brand made them seem. Or maybe the deal is good, but it returns every week, lasts only a few hours, or it’s available only with a premium membership. Alternatively, the deal might only be available from a retailer none of us has heard of or shopped at. Needless to say, we consider a ton of factors. With Black Friday coming up, you deserve transparency from us so you know — whether it’s this month or a random day in February — that you’re looking at an actual deal when you visit our site. The most basic criteria we use to judge whether a deal is good is whether we like the product enough to write about it and whether its price has dropped. Then we assess whether the discount is actually worth your attention. That part of the conversation has become a little complicated in the past year. RAMageddon and the ripple effects of higher tariffs have, in some cases, substantially impacted pricing and, by extension, the deals we cover. We follow deals closely enough to know when to bite at an offer or let it pass For products hit by recent price hikes, the new deal prices sometimes amount to the original sticker price, or close to it. Several of us would nod our heads with you if you think, “Hey, that’s not a deal; that’s just the original price. I’m no fool!” But it’s also technically a deal for many of us who are just trying to save wherever possible. Along those lines, we’ll sometimes highlight ways to save on digital or physical goods by buying discounted gift cards, which can be used to buy in-demand products. These methods are the only way to get any kind of deal on Grand Theft Auto VI before launch, for example. To help us stay aware of price drops, we also use free tracking tools like CamelCamelCamel and Keepa, which provide an independent read on Amazon’s historical pricing. (You can use them, too!) They’ll alert us when a product we like — and that we know you’ll probably like — goes on sale. Amazon also has its own Alexa for Shopping tool, which can show up to a year of pricing data and perform several other AI chatbot-like actions, including automatically buying products on your behalf. In my experience, Amazon’s historical pricing data usually aligns with non-Amazon-affiliated companies. However, none of them are perfect. Even the third-party tools we use don’t always display the record-low prices we’ve covered, for whatever reason. All of this to say, there are a lot of ins and outs, but we follow deals closely enough to know when to bite at an offer or let it pass. We cast a fairly large net for products across a range of categories ahead of the holidays, including some that don’t often get much play on The Verge. However, of the thousands of deals that we’ve seen ahead of Black Friday, you’re seeing the mere dozens of standouts that we’ve tested or used in our personal lives within each category — headphones, TVs, gaming accessories, smart home tech, etc. — that meet our criteria for being good products at noteworthy prices.

items.title: How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)
items.author: Denzil Correa
items.content: On November 17, 2026, the security research company Calif disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption vulnerability in the Base64 decoder of OpenJDK, the most widely used Java runtime. Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0, it scores 9.2 out of 10 (Critical). The flaw affects Java. OpenJDK published a security advisory and Oracle released patched builds in its November 2026 Critical Patch Update the same day, at 21:00 UTC. The vulnerability lets a remote attacker with no credentials send malformed Base64 data to a Java application and overwrite memory next to the decoded output. Calif turned that overwrite into a leak of heap memory, similar to Heartbleed, and into remote code execution. Calif demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution against Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate in their default configurations, and post-authentication remote code execution against Apache Kafka, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker. Cloudflare has released a new set of rules in the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset designed to detect malformed Base64 input patterns associated with this vulnerability. The rules are available on Pro, Business and Enterprise plans and are enabled by default with the Log action because malformed input and some benign application-specific token formats can resemble exploitation attempts. Blocking by default could therefore disrupt legitimate traffic. Customers can review matching requests in Security Events now and change the rules action to Block once they confirm it does not affect legitimate traffic. The WAF is an additional layer of defense, not a replacement for the patch. Java4Shell can be reached through paths a WAF does not see, like outbound TLS responses, and the only complete fix is to update the Java runtime. Our analysts continue to monitor attack activity and will update the rules as new techniques and variations appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and get more information on how the vulnerability develops on the dedicated Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing. We have seen no indication so far that Java4Shell was exploited on Cloudflare infrastructure. What we know about the vulnerability Base64 is a common way to represent binary data as text. Java applications decode Base64 when they process authentication headers, tokens, file uploads and many network messages. To decode it faster, OpenJDK replaces frequently used code with specialized machine code, called intrinsics. On supported x86-64 processors, the Base64 intrinsic uses AVX-512 instructions to process 64 bytes at a time. The bug sits in the handwritten assembly that handles the final characters of the input. When the tail of the input contains padding characters (=) in a position where valid Base64 never places them, the routine calculates a negative output length. That invalid length turns into a full 64-byte write. For a 65-character input, made of 64 characters followed by a single =, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte output array and then writes 62 bytes past its end. Java eventually rejects the input as invalid and throws an exception. By then, the neighboring memory has already been overwritten. An application's own input validation does not help, because the corruption happens inside the decoder before the application can reject the data. The simplest trigger is 64 A characters followed by =. On OpenJDK 17, the trigger needs 128 characters followed by =, because the threshold for the fast code path is higher. Exploitation is not point-and-shoot. The overwritten bytes are mostly fixed values, and the attacker controls only where the write lands. To build a working exploit, Calif arranged the Java heap so that the overflow enlarged neighboring arrays, which gave them first a way to read heap memory and then a way to write chosen bytes. Each target application requires its own exploit chain. Calif reported developing its first working local exploit in about three hours with the help of AI agents, so we expect other attackers to build exploit chains quickly. Who is affected Java4Shell affects a system only when all the following conditions are true: Condition Details Java runtime OpenJDK 17.0.6 or newer, including distributions built from OpenJDK: Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine, Red Hat OpenJDK, Oracle OpenJDK, Oracle Java SE and Oracle GraalVM for JDK. Check Oracle's advisory for the exact list of affected Oracle builds. Processor x86-64 with AVX-512 VBMI support, such as Intel Xeon Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids and Granite Rapids, or AMD EPYC and Ryzen Zen 4 or newer. ARM64 processors are not affected. Input The application decodes attacker-controlled Base64 data with the standard Java decoder. Many applications bundle their own Java runtime, and container images ship with a fixed Java Development Kit (JDK). Upgrading the system Java package does not update those copies, and it does not replace a Java virtual machine (JVM) that is already running. Every updated service needs a restart. Mitigate if you cannot patch right away If you cannot update immediately, Calif documents two JVM startup flags that remove the vulnerable code path: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics disables hardware-accelerated Base64 encoding and decoding. -XX:UseAVX=2 disables AVX-512. Apply this flag only on x86-64 hosts. OpenJDK on ARM does not recognize it and will fail to start. Both flags require a restart and may reduce performance for workloads that decode large amounts of Base64. They buy time while you patch. They do not replace the update. Protect your infrastructure while you patch Patching every Java runtime takes time, especially when JDKs are bundled inside applications and container images. Cloudflare WAF can reduce your exposure while you patch. A new managed rule, available on paid plans and enabled in Log mode by default, detects the malformed Base64 input that triggers Java4Shell. For Business and Enterprise customers, WAF attack score adds a machine learning layer that scores each request for remote code execution payloads, which helps catch variations and bypass attempts that signature-based rules can miss. New managed rules Protection for paid plans has been released as part of the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Ruleset ID efb7b8c949ac4650a09736fc376e9aee). The rule is enabled by default with the Log action, because blocking by default could cause false positives on legitimate Base64 traffic. To review its matches, go to Security > Security Analytics > Events and filter by the rule ID. If the matches are not legitimate traffic, change the rule action to Block: go to Security > Settings, edit the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, search for CVE-2026-114938 and set the rule action to Block. Alternatively, you can follow the link to review your configuration on the Zero Wire briefing. Rule description Rule ID Java4Shell - Malformed Base64 Header - CVE-2026-114938 5de9b20a45ea45d3841919ab4d718bf4 Java4Shell - Malformed Base64 Query Value - CVE-2026-114938 46bb4172813e471ea62d31c02337b51d Java4Shell - Malformed Base64 Body Value - CVE-2026-114938 d4dc3f71f1bc44a0811ae570e5e5836c Java4Shell - Malformed Base64 Path Segment - CVE-2026-114938 0dceaf0684b54fd0b085fcfb6fd6f152 Java4Shell - Malformed Base64url JWT Component - CVE-2026-114938 0ddd0eb664a040779f2f19065a25d991 Java4Shell - Malformed Base64 WebAuthn Value - CVE-2026-114938 4fce1ea79a614c07a27348d167d74ebb We are working on a rule for the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and will update this post when it is available. A WAF can block the exploit when the malformed Base64 arrives in an HTTP request that passes through Cloudflare. It cannot block every path to the vulnerable decoder, including: Encoded or nested data. The Base64 value may be wrapped inside another encoding or compressed format that the application unpacks before decoding. Non-HTTP protocols. Some affected products, such as the Apache Kafka broker, accept traffic over their own protocols. Outbound connections. Calif also shared a client-side exploit: a Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if it exposes no service of its own. Traffic that bypasses Cloudflare. This includes internal traffic between services. Adding defense-in-depth with WAF attack score While the managed rule is the primary way to block malformed Base64 triggers at the edge, Cloudflare WAF Attack Score (and specifically its remote code execution sub-score cf.waf.score.rce available on Enterprise plans) can offer an additional, complementary layer of protection. Because CVE-2026-114938 (Java4Shell) is a binary heap-corruption vulnerability, an attacker rarely achieves full, reliable remote code execution with a single 65-byte (or 129-byte) trigger string alone. On the wire, that initial trigger looks like an opaque, malformed Base64 string containing heap-corruption bytes rather than traditional web-layer injection syntax. As a result, machine learning models trained on application-layer injection patterns will not flag the raw Base64 trigger in isolation. Instead, turning a bounded JVM heap overflow into remote code execution over HTTP almost always requires a multi-stage or multi-parameter exploit chain, which creates more fingerprints that WAF Attack Score can inspect and flag, including: Heap Grooming and Triggering: To corrupt a predictable adjacent object on the JVM heap (such as a String or byte[] length header), attackers often send repetitive parameters or headers alongside the malformed Base64 payload to shape memory layout before triggering the out-of-bounds write. Second-Stage Payloads: Once heap corruption gives the attacker control over execution flow or object references, the exploit still needs commands, scripts, or Java gadgets to run. If an exploit chain pairs the initial heap-corruption trigger with a second-stage payload such as shell execution primitives (/bin/sh -c, cmd.exe, reverse-shell strings) or Java class-loading gadgets (java.lang.Runtime, ProcessBuilder, serialized object streams) tucked into another header, query parameter, or request body, cf.waf.score.rce can detect and score that secondary payload as malicious. Post-Exploitation Activity: Even if an initial heap-read or corruption request slips past edge filters, subsequent HTTP requests attempting to interact with an in-memory webshell or pass OS commands to the compromised JVM remain directly visible to WAF Attack Score. Deploy protections and patch Because sophisticated in-memory exploits can still execute raw shellcode or manipulate bytecode without ever sending plaintext shell commands over HTTP, WAF Attack Score should be used alongside explicit Base64 rules and JVM patching. You can find more information on how to deploy Managed rules and attack score in our WAF guide, but in a nutshell: 1. Set the CVE-2026-114938 rule in the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Pro plan and above) to Block. It is enabled in Log mode by default, so review its matches in Security Events first. Use the links on the Cloudflare Zero Wire page to review your rules status. 2. Layer Attack Score to get ML-based remote code execution (RCE) detection: create a custom rule blocking or challenging requests with a low RCE attack score (for example, cf.waf.score.rce le 20 on Enterprise plans, or cf.waf.score.class eq "attack" on Business plans) to catch multi-stage exploit chains and post-exploitation command traffic. 3. Remediate at runtime: Upgrade to patched OpenJDK builds (or set -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as a temporary workaround) to eliminate the vulnerable AVX-512 code path entirely. Follow the OpenJDK advisory and Oracle's Critical Patch Update and install your Java vendor's fixed release as soon as possible. For a prompt you can give an AI agent to inventory your Java runtimes, see the Java4Shell page on Cloudflare Zero Wire. Impact on Cloudflare infrastructure Cloudflare also runs Java, so when Java4Shell was disclosed we checked our own systems. The vulnerability can only be triggered in specific hardware configurations, namely a x86-64 processor that supports AVX-512 VBMI, so a system is exposed only when both are true. Our investigation found that the majority of our Java workloads are not scheduled on vulnerable systems; we took immediate action to protect the remainder. About an hour after the patches were published, we began rolling out a JVM startup option that turns off the accelerated Base64 routine containing the bug on all Java workloads, so decoding falls back to the standard implementation. To be safe, we are rolling out our patched configuration to all machines, regardless of hardware as a precaution. We have seen no indication so far that Java4Shell was exploited on Cloudflare infrastructure. Update every Java runtime now Java4Shell turns a performance optimization in the Java runtime into a path to remote code execution, and with technical details now public, we expect exploit attempts to follow quickly. The fix is to update every Java runtime and restart the services that use it. While you patch, review the new managed rule's matches and switch it to Block if you are on a paid plan and use attack score to catch remote code execution payloads that signatures may miss. Our WAF analysts will continue to update protections as new techniques emerge. Follow the WAF changelog for rule updates and the Java4Shell page on Cloudflare Zero Wire for the latest on this vulnerability.

items.content: Do automated license plate readers (ALPRs) have any place in our communities? That question has been a hot topic in city council meetings, community conversations, and news coverage around the country for months. This past election day, a couple of U.S communities took it further: to the ballot. And overwhelmingly, voters decided that, no, these devices should not be deployed on our streets. We agree! In Maine, the coastal community of York voted to remove the town’s existing ALPR cameras and require that any future proposed installations receive voter approval before proceeding. The local initiative ended up on the ballot after constituents gathered enough signatures on a citizens’ petition for a local ordinance. On Election Day, nearly three-quarters of York voters supported the ban. Thousands of miles away, voters in League City, Texas also voted against allowing the local police department to continue use of ALPR cameras. That vote was formally approved on November 17, which began a 72-hour window to remove the cameras. Since the election, the cameras have been “bagged” or covered to prevent the collection of data. At least one city also decided to expand protections afforded to their residents when it comes to the use of surveillance technology. In Pflugerville, Texas, Proposition B passed, now requiring that the City Charter be amended to include “protections governing the collection, use, retention, and oversight of data, facial recognition, and surveillance technologies.” It also requires “a responsible artificial intelligence framework.” While every municipality has different rules for how to get a local ordinance placed on the ballot, banning use and securing the removal of surveillance tools locally is a powerful way of protecting your community against devices and data collection that goes far beyond your town lines. Surveillance is a choice, not a mandate, and our communities have the power to refuse it. EFF has supported local communities around the country over the last few years in advocating against the procurement of surveillance technologies in their cities, counties, and states. These victories at the ballot box and in city councils show that when mass surveillance is presented as a policy choice, not a technical necessity, communities can and do reject it. Do you know what surveillance tools are being used by your local police departments? Check out the Atlas of Surveillance to learn more about the tools deployed in your city, and sign up to volunteer if you want to push for more transparency across the country.

items.title: Surveillance Isn't Safety: A Comic About Organizing Against Flock and Other Foes
items.author: Dave Maass
items.content: In the new comic "Surveillance Isn't Safety"—available for free today— cartoonist Bryn Adams explores the growing movement against mass surveillance through their involvement in the community fight against Flock Safety in Cleveland, Ohio. It's a personal journey that will resonate widely with residents in hundreds of cities where communities are drawing the line against automated license plate readers (ALPRs). Jump to the Comic Or download the PDF Published in collaboration between EFF and Crucial Comix, Bryn's comic captures the authenticity of the grassroot backlash against the surveillance industry—undercutting Flock founder Garrett Langley's latest dubious defense that public opposition of his company's product isn't real. At the International Association of Chiefs of Police conference this fall, Langley accused the anti-surveillance activism of being driven by Russian bots and as being "inorganic." He pointed to the fact that many local groups were using similar language in their protest signs as supposed proof, when in reality, shared slogans are one of the hallmarks of a social movement. This was all misdirection from the grim realities that Flock and other ALPR systems facilitate: the mistakes are real; the abuse is real; the racism is real; and the targeting of dissenters, migrants, and abortion seekers is real. And, importantly, the cancelled contracts are real. Bryn's comic sheds light on the real abuses and threats driving communities to mobilize against Flock, Axon, and other ALPR vendors. It shows that coast-to-coast activism doesn't happen overnight—any more than a comic appears out of thin air as a finished product. As advisors on the cartoon, EFF watched how Bryn's script evolved from rough sketches to penciled drawings, then to inked and shaded panels, mirroring how the long-running movement against mass surveillance has steadily snowballed over the last few years. There is nothing “inorganic” about either: Both are built on passion, commitment, and putting in the work. items.title: Quickly, There’s No Time
items.author: TheZvi
items.content: In response to the METR report, many people have been reevaluating their timelines. Two prominent reactions are a new timelines update from the AI Futures Project, and the new predictions of Paul Christiano (day 1, day 2, day 3), who gave three days of talks about our current situation and also sat down with Dwarkesh Patel. This post covers the updates from the AI Futures Project, Dwarkesh Patel and Paul Christiano, as well as some others, and a post about RSI nomenclature and approach from Dean Ball. I will be following this up soon with full coverage of the related podcast between Paul Christiano and Dwarkesh Patel. In that podcast, Paul Christiano predicts we are on pace for very rapid progress very soon, with potential takeover by AIs within 6-12 months, and he calls on us to pause until we have alignment and security in a much better place. Table of Contents The Latest Update and Current Situation in Broad Terms. Time Until What? Quickly, There’s No Time. Paul Christiano Sees Takeover Risk Within a Year. Dwarkesh Patel Now Expects Superintelligence by 2030. Other People’s Updates. There Are Many Skeptics. Wow, That Escalated Quickly. Dean Ball Skies Down the Slope. Safety Is a Limiting Factor. No, This Is Not a Strawman. We Need a Plan That Meets the Moment. The Latest Update and Current Situation in Broad Terms These updates towards shorter timelines seem directionally correct to me. There is a substantial chance that we will see superintelligence developed, that can fully automate AI R&D (SAR) or even do all digital tasks (TED-AI), in 2027. Contra the AI Futures Project I believe an SAR in 2027 is under 50% to happen, but not so far under 50%. It would be surprising to me but not shocking if we do nothing to slow down and still do not see something close to an SAR by the end of 2028. If you do not have an importantly non-zero chance of the development of superintelligence in 2027, I believe you are making a clear mistake. I worry that some are overreacting, and taking this too far too fast, and treating full superintelligence 2027 as a baseline scenario rather than a possibility. I reiterate that a lot of these updates feel like people fixing their failure to update previously. Did you need three people from METR in order to believe the things that Anthropic and OpenAI are saying about their internal pace of development? What did you expect a METR report from inside Anthropic to say? Were you not paying attention? Are you this sensitive to the exact set of points on the AECI graph? You should have made a lot of these updates months ago. Past predictive failures are not what is important. What matters is what happens next. You should be prepared for AI capabilities to advance rapidly in 2027, far more rapidly than in previous years, including the potential for superintelligence and fully strong recursive self-improvement. It is a realistic possibility, although unlikely, that humanity could pass the full point of no return or de facto lose control over the future during 2027, or that life could become seriously disrupted in highly unpleasant ways. If your plan presumes that it has more time than this then it is not a good plan. I have not seen a plan that could make superintelligence likely to go well, if that superintelligence gets built in 2027. We need more time. You should also be prepared if recursive self-improvement and superintelligence do not arrive in 2027. There are many things that could impact how fast things go, or what it would take to achieve full RSI or superintelligence. Our observations of the past are noisy. When trying to predict an exponential, small changes in how fast things accelerate can become dramatic differences in when or how things happen. If your plan presumes the crucial events happen in 2027, and fails without a fallback if things take longer than that, then this too is not a good plan. It is also possible that we will take collective action, either among the labs or via governments, to limit the rate of capability advances, via pacing of the frontier or even outright pausing development of frontier AI. If so, these timelines become longer. Time Until What? Different people are talking about different things. Careful ones will be precise. Timelines refers to how long we expect it to take to reach various transformational milestones in AI. Typically, these days, what we are measuring is the time until some definition of a form of superintelligence (ASI), typically meaning something of the form ‘AIs that will be able to do approximately all of the things better than you.’ We can also talk about particular capabilities. The AI Futures Project, the team behind AI 2027, talks about the Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) that can narrowly take over AI research, and the Top-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI) that could automate all white-collar work. Because of recursive self-improvement (RSI), once you have an SAR you can use that to build better AIs, so you quickly end up with a TED-AI or a traditional ASI. We then sometimes talk about any of these, or things in between: Time until the development of some AI system with particular capabilities. Time until some impact in the physical world. Time until the Point of No Return, when for practical purposes human decisions can no longer change how things play out from there. Time until AI has taken over AI R&D and humans are functionally out of the loop. Time until visible AI takeover, where the AIs are clearly in charge. Time until we are each and every one of us actually and physically dead. There are good reasons to care about all of these timelines. Sof 𓋹: to some extent intelligence is being able to patch the ways in which you are not intelligent RSI is not technically one singular moment, in the sense that there is not one fixed time at 8:52am on a Tuesday when it happens or starts. It is still highly useful to think of there being a point where RSI has clearly begun in earnest, with humans increasingly out of the loop and the pace of progress accelerating such that we should expect further progress to rapidly continue to accelerate, where progress begets more progress faster, and this is expected to continue for at least what previously would have been many years of progress. Similarly, even though there is unlikely to be that one particular moment when you press ‘Y/N’ on SkyNet, and instead our loss of ability to change course will be more gradual, we can still usefully speak of a Point of No Return, or a point of takeover. Dead, on the other hand, is dead. Quickly, There’s No Time The AI 2027 team’s timelines have shrunk dramatically in the wake of the METR report. The full post is very detailed. I recommend reading it in full if and only if you care a lot about such details. Benchmark trends and other observations were expected to if anything slow down. Instead they have accelerated, in ways that Daniel Kokotajlo had as ~4% to happen. This puts us well ahead of the original AI 2027 timeline. There is a lot of talk about ‘research taste’ as the main limiting factor. Humans are for now needed because they come up with superior ideas, and have superior research taste. If and when that changes, the rest follows. We would get SARs, capable of doing all parts of the research, but the result of their work would probably become increasingly misaligned through cycles of development. Again, if you want to get into all the mechanics of the various modeling decisions and lines on graphs and their implications, read the report. If you want the summary version, the rest of this section provides that. Eli Lifland: METR estimates nearly 2x acceleration in Anthropic’s progress due to AI. That’s a big deal: My previous median for Superhuman AI Researcher was ~2030, now it’s 2027. I feel very worried that humanity might no longer be in control of our future within 3-12 months. j⧉nus: 3 months would be wild. I’m here for it. what if we already lost control 3 months ago? j⧉nus: “I feel very worried that humanity might no longer be in control of our future within 3-12 months.” i am curious what people mean when they say “humanity no longer in control” if they’re thinking of something concrete, like “if humans try to shut down AI, they will prevent it” roon (OpenAI): yes its confusing because some people are using this as a euphemism for total human extinction, and others are using it more mildly for something like gradual disempowerment They offer a wide variety of different ways of extrapolating and analyzing the data. The answers differ somewhat, but all point to the conclusion that things are going to accelerate quite a lot and do so very soon. Daniel Kokotajlo: Unfortunately, it seems like the intelligence explosion will be happening in 2027 after all. Most of this post analyzes the new METR report (though other sources of evidence are also important). If they’re right, that implies an AI-driven acceleration that is 5 months ahead of the AI 2027 scenario. I am scared, sad, and angry. Eli Lifland: METR recently estimated that Anthropic is now making AI progress about twice as fast as its historical rate (they would not be surprised by anything from 1.3x to 3x), and guessed that “perhaps ≈80%” of the current acceleration is due to AI. If they’re right, that implies an AI-driven acceleration that is 5 months ahead of the AI 2027 scenario. … Now, all of us forecast that Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) will likely arrive at some point in 2027 (assuming no substantial deliberate slowdown). We also predict a 35-65% chance that Top-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI), AIs that can automate all white-collar work, will arrive before 2028. While there were many factors and sources of evidence that influenced us, the single biggest source was the METR report. If SAR is coming in 2027, it is incredibly urgent to pause or substantially ‘pace’ frontier AI development, with the ideal being an industry-wide pause followed by an international agreement. Why is the pace of progress accelerating this rapidly? This question is a huge deal and it likely makes sense to return to them for a more in-depth look when I have the time. Alas right now I am under a severe time crunch due to a combination of trips and Fable 5.2, as well as other news. All of this is a pretty big change: If you want to avoid the conclusion that we will get to SAR and TED-AI within the next few years, you need there to be some particular reason why this happens. Trends have to break. Like Moore’s Law and other such trends, the trends do not hold merely because you feed more numbers into the number-go-up machine. The trends hold because we find continual improvements and innovations, including step changes. That is how the trends have continued this long. There are various versions of ‘the AIs will need [X] and won’t have it’ as explanations for why all of this won’t happen. Those types of methods have predicted ~7 of the last zero times that AI has hit a wall and stopped advancing its capabilities. They have looked rather foolish. None of the remaining barriers seem different in kind to me than the barriers already overcome. None of them seem like showstoppers. For most of them it even seems rather obvious, in broad terms, how one gets around them or goes straight through them. Directionally the report seems correct to me. I worry that the updates are too large, but yes in a broad sense this is what peak prediction performance looks like. When the facts change you change your mind, in both directions. Paul Christiano Sees Takeover Risk Within a Year Paul Christiano now sees ‘meaningful risk’ of AI takeover within 6-12 months. This is up from his previous estimate back in September of only 4% chance of loss of control within one year and 15% within three years. This was doubtless heavily influenced by what he saw inside OpenAI after joining, not only the METR report. Paul Christiano, a member of OpenAI’s board of directors, then calls in his personal capacity for AI companies to pause development of AI until we can first greatly improve our security and alignment capabilities. Rob Wiblin: Paul Christiano (OpenAI board member) yesterday: “There’s material risk of AI takeover in the next 6-12 months. We have seen roughly the things we might expect to see shortly before something really bad were to happen. Even with [any] realistic policy responses, the risk remains exceptionally high. If we build this as quickly as we can in the easiest way we can the chance is [more like] a coin flip [within the next 3 years]. For most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident.” Christiano: • Is on OpenAI’s safety and security committee (which exists to block risky practices) • Co-invented RLHF at OpenAI back in 2017-2021 • From 2024-2026 was head of safety at the US gov’s AI agency (now called CAISSI) (Video is from ‘The Hinton Lectures’ there’s another on tonight and tomorrow.) This, as Janus notices, is a strange use of the word ‘accident.’ If you die via this AI ‘accident’ then the ‘accident’ is that we lost control over the AIs and with them the future, or the AIs engaged in destructive actions. This is an ‘accident’ in the sense that it was a mistake to allow that to happen, and we doubtless messed up along the way, but no, this does not count as an ‘accident.’ As Douglas Adams might put it, that is throwing yourself at the ground and not missing. Whoops. Face plant. Also death. What this post does not cover is the full podcast Christiano did with Patel. I will be covering that post on its own soon. Dwarkesh Patel Now Expects Superintelligence by 2030 Dwarkesh Patel does a good job cutting to the heart of what is likely coming. His new median year for human-level automated AI researchers is 2028, with a 25% chance it comes after 2032, which means his median for everything after that is soon after 2028. AI research is a lot like math in that you can do it by making number go up. AIs are going to get very good at AI research. We will then be able to make massive progress on AI research. That will be good enough to make AIs better than us at everything else. I too believe this is the core story. Yes, these other capabilities will lag well behind coding, math and AI research, in terms of AI’s relative capabilities. That won’t matter. What matters is that they will keep going up in absolute terms. What also matters is that if the way you solve AI research is by focusing on number going up, then hope for successful alignment is somewhere between slim and none. The way to optimize any given number will reliably get you killed. I worry that his claim that AI R&D is largely verifiable is true to about the worst possible extent. That you can do a lot by making number go up, but that this inevitably becomes perverse at the limit. Dwarkesh Patel: Maybe to summarize the basic argument of this essay a different way: Current AIs are spiky and jagged – worse than humans in most domain, but often as good, or better, in ones with verifiable proxies (for example, math). One such verifiable domain (I argue) is AI research. And while the first AIs that dramatically accelerate AI progress will be quite narrow (i.e. probably not able to automate most jobs), the consequences of that accelerated progress will be very general. And that’s because better learning algorithms are very general. For example, GPT-6 (while still being jagged) is just way, way better than GPT-3 at practically everything. I’m arguing that we’re only a couple years away (and possibly only a couple months away) from a process by which (initially) narrow AIs concentrate a jump as big as the one from GPT-3 to GPT-6 into a single year. And if you got another jump that big, but starting from the base of GPT-7, I think you would end up with AIs that would rapidly become better than the best humans in every field. The question has always been when this happens. For a while I’ve heard Dwarkesh do podcasts in which he expects this process to be slow. He would cite various supposed bottlenecks and requirements, often involving the need for continual learning (link goes to his mea culpa on that) or making connections across fields. I’ve many times questioned his reasoning on that. Now he’s changed his mind. Good. Dwarkesh Patel: If you asked me earlier this year how far away we are from superintelligence, I’d probably have said at least the better part of a decade. But over the last three months, I’ve updated my views a ton. I’ve been debating people about this question, both on and off the podcast. And I’ve been watching the progress of AI on verifiable domains and thinking about what that implies for AI research itself. I’ve now come to the view that we’re only a couple of years away, and possibly only a couple of months away, from AIs that are as good as the best humans at AI research. Dwarkesh then goes over various points that I think of as obvious, but which are indeed true objections people raise. He has an extended section to explain that yes, automating the best researchers would speed up AI progress a lot. He also has to explain that superintelligence would be a really good meta-learner, because people somehow think otherwise. One ‘hope’ in this style of model is that we might get a ‘spark’ rather than a singularity. As in, a big jump that then stalls out, without turning into a world beyond human comprehension, perhaps because of the ‘ideas get harder to find’ issue. He gives the spark scenario about a 50% chance. That seems far too high to me. If it did happen, that would potentially be amazingly great. Joshua Saxe, a longtime skeptic of RSI claims, had high praise for Dwarkesh’s essay. Joshua Saxe: Bravo, this is the clearest plausible mechanism for an RSI takeoff I’ve seen, and has made me much less of an RSI skeptic. Previously I’d been hung up on the fact that so much of model post-training requires humans in the loop to shape post-training data and RL environments to make the models economically valuable (e.g. if you’re hill climbing a model’s ability to make Powerpoint slides, or TV commercials, or to plan vacations in Italy, you need a human in the loop shaping the data and RL environments until you get a value-producing outcome). Dwarkesh focuses on the part of RSI that’d involve hill climbing the learning algorithms themselves so that we get models that generalize better from their training and in-context data, optimizing not the model’s value producing tasks but their ability to learn them more data and compute efficiently. I love that this gives us a clear definition based in technical plausibility. A few next steps would move the discourse further .. one would be to actually get data on what the economic returns on this kind of learning algorithm hill climbing actually are, and whether these are sufficient to incentivize the capital markets to fund an intelligence explosion. The capital/value cycle is, after all, the outer loop of most intelligence explosion scenarios and it appears RSI under this definition will be quite expensive. Another parallel thing would be to get data on whether Dwarkesh’s mechanism is showing up empirically in AI research today and to what extent, to set timelines. Unfortunately the relevant data are hidden and writing in this area is as a result too vague. To wit, I would like to fit something like Chinchilla scaling laws to the closed labs models, and see how these are changing over time, but I can’t, because I don’t know key quantities like parameter counts, pretraining compute volume, and pretraining loss (and couldn’t normalize between the various labs’ pretraining datasets). Without these mechanisms we’re stuck inferring hidden variables from outside observables like performance on downstream evals that aren’t the point — as I take it — of the theory being proposed here. This response is emblematic of a type of thinking that wants to focus on particular mechanisms, and demands, while being one of us dumber slower things, to know exactly how the smarter faster things will improve upon the ways of the dumber slower things, and to see parallels of it being implemented now by us and working. Things are so overdetermined that you can satisfy such requirements, but you should expect what that kind of thinking expects to be greatly exceeded by what the smarter things actually end up doing. Dwarkesh called for good counterarguments in this thread. I have been highly unimpressed by what responses I have seen. Other People’s Updates Nate Soares (MIRI): I’m not as worried about short AI timelines as some others are. For instance, I think it’s more likely than not that we make it to 2028. >50% chance. don’t get ahead of yourself. Geoffrey Hinton warns EU leaders that AI could kill us in three years and refers to Paul Christiano’s warnings. Geoffrey Hinton: I go to Paul’s lectures and he sort of says, this stuff might happen in the next 18 months. And that’s terrifying. Buck Shlegeris predicts a one in three chance of superintelligence within a year. If this does happen, he expects the resulting AIs to take over with a serious chance all or most humans will be killed. He predicts ~20% chance that within a year misalignment issues prevent you from living your life normally due to being dead or enslaved or due to collateral damage. Neel Nanda: I respect Buck’s judgement, and he’s often been more right than me on what needs to happen in AI Safety. Seeing him conclude things like this is very concerning. What would cause Buck to admit he was wrong? His guess as to how he could be importantly wrong would be if, contra METR’s report, the reason for increased AI capability gains was mainly access to more compute, rather than other factors. One simple way to project is to task what percentage of Anthropic R&D tasks are AL4 or already at AL5, as in fully led by Claude. Andrew Curran: Sam McCandlish said five days ago that Anthropic would be releasing a report on the speed of internal progress, so we will finally get an update to this chart. I’m very interested to see what this number is now. [AI Futures Project] thinks it is at 50%. AL4 is the last step before full RSI. Peter Wildeford: My median is that we’ve already reached 80% AL4. And that we probably have like 1% AL5 though maybe they’re holding out from doing that. 墨尔本Will: 80% is insane! By holding out do you mean you think Anthropic will be pacing at AL5? Peter Wildeford: Yes If I had to guess I would say that 50% here is a bit high and it was at the time more like 40%, but we are in the steep part of the sigmoid so it could shoot up. There Are Many Skeptics Most people out there remain skeptics. The vast majority of people do not expect superintelligence to arrive any time soon. Their reasons for skepticism vary, as does the quality of those reasons. One can divide objections into roughly ten categories. People who don’t know what current AIs can do (not AI pilled). People who don’t understand that AIs will improve (not AGI pilled). I’m not listening, la la la. That or belief in it would be inconvenient or unfortunate, so it won’t happen. People who dismiss this all via absurdity heuristic, ‘nothing ever happens,’ drawing inapplicable parallels to past technological improvements, or who say something isomorphic to ‘until you get full RSI you have not done RSI so you haven’t shown you can do RSI,’ aka ‘I’ll believe it when I see it’ or ‘how about we stop just after someone gets hurt,’ etc. People who cite the market, or experts, or say advocates are weird or low status. We will not get full recursive self-improvement (RSI) and progress will be slow. We will get RSI, but it will ‘peter out’ due to difficulty rising faster than efficiency. We will get narrow AI R&D ASI and RSI in verifiable domains with data, but this won’t translate to other domains. We will ‘hit walls’ or be unable to do tasks that are too ‘messy’ or that lack the proper training data, and so on. Intelligence denialism: Intelligence doesn’t much matter (not ASI pilled). It would be beyond scope, and I would be repeating myself, to fully address these. The first five objections, as should be obvious, are exceptionally poor. The best objections, to me, are in #7 and #8, and to some extent #9. There are also a much larger number of bad objections in these categories, which often assume future AI will use exactly current training techniques and only be used to exactly substitute for existing methods and never invent or change anything or work around obstacles or make leaps. In general #6 is a fine thing to notice but it gets overridden by other evidence. I get especially frustrated by #10, where many people really should know better. Wow, That Escalated Quickly Things are, as they say, escalating quickly. Compare now to predictions in January. Raymond Arnold points out that, metaphorically similarly to a sports overtime, we are in ‘epistemic sudden death.’ As in, your next meaningful observation about AI might mean it is too late, and you lose, as in everyone dies. Dean Ball Skies Down the Slope A standard issue with talk about any accelerating process is the slippery slope. We all agree that too much or too intense [X], here RSI, is bad. And we all agree that some amount of some weak version of it is good, or at least not similarly bad. This risks a slippery slope in both directions, and it risks both a conflation of different things and also risks false distinctions. We absolutely need to speak carefully here. In light of that, Dean Ball suggests we split RSI talk into weak versus strong. Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): Let’s start by making one thing clear: allowing AI to control the development of its successors with no or little practical human oversight—essentially, handing over the keys of America’s largest AI companies to AI—is a bad idea. No matter how useful AI is for accelerating AI R&D, humans should remain in control, not just in name but in actual fact, over the development of AI. No amount of technological progress is worth the forfeiture of practical human control over AI companies, or, for that matter, of other human institutions. I support the development of laws, regulations, and norms to enforce this worldwide. But this risk—a relatively narrow one—isn’t what current conversations about RSI focus on in practice. To understand what I mean, it’s helpful to think of two distinct ways in which a technology might recursively improve itself. I’ll call these weak recursion and strong recursion. The weak version is normal technology. Weak recursion is when a technology is a key input into the production of more and better versions of that same technology. It is an extremely common pattern in technology development—really it is the historical norm rather than an aberration. Iron Age metalsmiths used iron as one of the key inputs to make more iron, and stronger alloys of it too. Weak recursion has been a crucial driver of human technological progress over centuries and millennia, and in this sense there is nothing especially weak about it. The strong version is very different. Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): Strong recursion is when a technology can autonomously plan and execute the development of its successor. As far as we know, strong recursion has never happened at any point in history. Well, perhaps it happened once. The technology is called humanity, or even life. Each generation builds the next one. We do have a bit of an existence proof. But we digress. Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): Strong recursion would be a genuinely new thing under the sun. We should take this possibility seriously, but one part of taking a thing seriously is to adhere to rigorous epistemic discipline in analysis. Thus, one should not jump to the conclusion that “recursive self-improvement is happening” if that recursion is of the weak variety instead of the strong. It’s only (strong) recursive self-improvement if it exists in its pure form, where humans do not touch anything in the process. Otherwise, this line of thinking goes, it’s a normal process. I agree that there is something special about full no-humans-in-the-loop, but surely you should be able to understand the danger and non-normality of what is happening if AI is already doubling the rate of AI progress now, and is likely to then begin doubling it again, and each doubling looks to be faster than the previous one. Humans being decreasingly or nominally ‘in the loop’ slows this down some, but perhaps not very much. This can remind us of the old Yudkowsky-Christiano debates between ‘slow’ takeoff that takes months or years to transform the world, similar in this case to Dean Ball’s weak recursion, versus ‘fast’ takeoff that takes even less time than that. We currently are in a ‘slow’ takeoff world, Christino is saying so himself, and we are seeing exactly how not slow that is. More to the point, Dean’s weak recursion is the precursor to strong recursion, or at least steadily stronger recursion. That’s what METR was centrally trying to point out. Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): The METR study of Anthropic’s internal R&D acceleration is undeniably good evidence that weak recursion is taking place. But is it evidence that strong recursion is underway? It depends how you look at it. METR’s finding is specifically that Anthropic has doubled the rate at which its models’ capabilities improve on well-specified tasks, which makes one wonder who, exactly, is doing the specifying. I would say no, in the sense that strong recursion or fast takeoff is in the future. I would say yes, in the sense that this is predictive of that happening in the future, and how soon in the future that might happen. Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): Now, as I said, weak recursion is not really weak: it is one of the most powerful dynamics in human history, rhyming if not synonymous with the concept of compounding growth. The whole ‘only on well-specified tasks’ thing continues to strike me as excessively weak sauce, a Hayekian copium that thinks that specification cannot be solved. And yet, Dean acknowledges that strong recursion might arrive soon. Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): My view is that strong recursion is a genuine risk, possibly in the near term, though the evidence for it is thinner than is sometimes supposed. The cautionary argument is, essentially, that there is a loop, so the AI has to do this set of many tasks that constitute the loop in order to take humans out of it, and some of those tasks will be hard for AI to do. I think this both vastly underestimates superintelligence (a continual disagreement I have with Dean) and also presumes too much about inability to alter loop components. There is the whole ‘real world’ objection, and also the ‘strategic choice’ or ‘research taste’ objections, as per usual. I feel these are far more ‘we are not yet on the steep part of the S-curve’ and ‘this is lagging behind other skills by mostly constant amounts’ situations than actual permanent deficits versus humans, but this post is not the place to rehash those questions. Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): And it requires AI that can do all those things not in some abstract space, but in the real world, where information is imperfect and resources are scarce. … It is true that AI improves rapidly, but much of what I have described above has remained elusive to even the best AI systems. … It is unclear how we would even design evaluations for long-range intellectual taste. What is Dean trying to head off here? Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): But do the risks of weak recursion justify banning the practice of using AI as an input to make more and better AI? In my view, they do not. … What’s more, weak recursion with AI can be used to make AI systems safer. … The kind of panic that today’s rhetoric could provoke could easily result in laws that delay legitimate and desirable benefits of AI, put the U.S. at a strategic disadvantage on the global stage, and centralize power over AI in the hands of the state. The correct response to worries about an overreaction is to help design the correct reaction, now, before the overreaction happens. All the options we know about have severe flaws. Indefinitely doing nothing has flaws that are far worse, whether or not it is too late for a crackdown when we finally want to overreact. Banning all use of any form of AI in improving AI is very close to banning improving AI. It is damn near impossible to make progress on AI under that kind of rule. Banning RSI means something short of that. We can and must talk price. What we cannot do is say that because some amount of AI will get used anyway, we can’t define a rule and thus simply have to accept unlimited intensity and quantity of RSI. Nor do I think that the ‘existing law and liability can handle this’ arguments hold much water for AI risks in general, let alone a true RSI situation. In a true RSI situation it is kind of a joke to say that maybe down the line you might get sued. Safety Is a Limiting Factor The quote below could read as ‘OpenAI could be automating its R&D process more.’ If you are unaware that models on the level of Astra can automate substantial portions of the AI R&D process, and are meaningfully accelerating AI R&D, then yes, that part of Altman’s statement dominates. This would, to you, be an important update. Given that I already knew that, I see it instead primarily as ‘OpenAI cannot yet be automating its R&D process more than they are, and might have gone too far too fast.’ If they try, the resulting models will be too misaligned to be useful or release, with a high chance of causing an incident as bad as Hugging Face or worse. Which may or may not have already happened. prinz: I’ve spent much of the day noodling over what Sam Altman meant when he said that OpenAI “could be pushing more towards the RSI spectrum than we are”. Would seem to suggest that OpenAI’s models can now perform some portion of AI R&D fully autonomously, with no human oversight? Full quote: “Are we developing new models faster than we would without using our technology? Yes. Are we pushing a button and just saying, ‘Hey, model, like, design the next version and rapidly self-improve with no human oversight?’ Definitely not. We could be pushing more towards the RSI spectrum than we are, but I don’t think we could safely do that.” Exactly. They could not safely do that. I would like to think of this as OpenAI recognizing the existential risks involved. There may be some of that, but I see Altman as mainly saying something practical. If you keep pushing the ‘have the AI do a bunch of these things for you’ buttons, things go faster, but you do not get ‘operational excellence’ and you get an increasing amount of misalignment difficulties. This is probably not because Astra is actively sabotaging you. This is mostly a Skill Issue. No, This Is Not a Strawman I am very worried that people will say ‘well you predicted that big dangerous things might happen in 2027 and gave it a 25% chance, but it is now 2028 and it did not happen, so you have been proven wrong and this means nothing will ever happen.’ Seriously, this happens all the time, including straight up. Tom Chivers: Sure, this guy is predicting AI doom in the next year, but he was predicting AI doom in ten years nine years ago, and it hasn’t happened yet. There are a bunch of common variations of this. Let [X] be some bad thing. Here are ten examples of things people often say. Each of these ends ‘therefore you lose all credibility and [X] will never happen.’ You said that by now there was a [10% / 25% / 50%] chance of [X]. You used to say [X] would happen [sooner/later], now you say [later/sooner]. You used to say [X] would happen [more/less] often, now you say [less/more] often. You mentioned that [Y] might happen before [X], but [Y] hasn’t happened. You did not sufficiently loudly say that [X] also might not happen. The market does not predict [X], if [X] was going to happen we would see [Y]. (usually in a way that would make no sense even if the market really did believe it). If you really believed [X] you would (do a thing that makes no sense and is often morally abominable, or make a trade that makes no sense, etc). If you really believed [X] you would (do a thing that only makes sense if [X] is 99%+ to happen, which you did not predict.) If [X] happened that would be weird or bad or surprising or whatever. [X] would be something happening, whereas we all know nothing ever happens. Or it would require intelligence enabling some new thing we do not currently know how to do, which sounds like science fiction. And so on. You will continue to see such arguments, usually from people who have continuously made now-falsified predictions about AI. Do not listen to them. We Need a Plan That Meets the Moment A lot of evidence is in. Many things point to the substantial possibility of superintelligence in 2027: Extrapolation from the AECI and many other metrics of AI capabilities, as per the analysis of the AI Futures Project. METR’s report from inside Anthropic. Widespread claims, against interest, both from OpenAI and Anthropic employees as well as many official communications. The analysis of many who have previously made highly accurate predictions about AI capabilities. The forecast, in particular, of Paul Christiano. There are also reasons for skepticism as well. Many remain skeptical. Most reasons for skepticism are ignorance of the evidence, or failure to consider the evidence, but there are also better arguments. I am taking many of those better arguments into consideration, as well as the potential for model error. This is why I continue to believe that the probability of full automation of AI R&D in 2027 is under 50%. In order to meet this moment, any plan has to be ready for the full automation of AI R&D inside Anthropic or OpenAI, and perhaps beyond that, by the end of 2027, resulting in rapid RSI and advancement in AI capabilities beyond human levels. The most obvious plan is to slow or pause advancements in AI capabilities. Here is a thread of a few of the people supporting this: Nate Silver, Elizabeth Warren, the Financial Times editorial board, Ezra Klein, Eric Hoel, Robert Wiblin, Rutger Bregman, Peggy Noonan and Abdul El-Sayed. Any plan that works on that time frame needs to include mechanisms to slow down the resulting growth in capabilities. We also need to be as ready as we can for when and if those capabilities arrive, including what happens if that development goes well. We would then face a host of other urgent and deadly problems. The plan also cannot assume that this will happen. We cannot stop planning for futures in which AI capabilities only advance a smaller amount without anything we could call a takeoff. And also, yes, we need to be ready for the possibility that radical improvement in AI capabilities might not upend things as much as I expect that they would, or do so as fast as I would expect that to happen. We could still blow the ‘easy’ worlds. We cannot and must not burn our seed corn, of any type, until and unless we get much stronger evidence, either personally or globally, that we are in a world where we need to do that. It’s a marathon, folks. Until it isn’t.

items.title: Waymo has stopped its robotaxis from driving on the freeway—here’s why
items.author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
items.content: Waymo is currently restricting its fleet of robotaxis to surface streets after getting into hot water with California over its cars' driving behavior on highways. Specifically, the software tends to drive into construction zones at speed. As first reported by the San Francisco Business Times, this behavior actually drew the ire of California’s DMV earlier this month, which ordered Waymo to stop driving on Californian highways immediately and until it can convince the DMV that its cars no longer “pose an imminent hazard to public safety.” This is not Waymo’s first run-in with this problem. In Arizona, Waymo robotaxis did not recognize ramp closure signs on six occasions in Phoenix in April and entered construction zones. A month later in California, seven Waymo robotaxis entered lanes with active construction. In June, Waymo recalled the almost 3,800 robotaxis capable of highway driving. That problem led Waymo to stick to surface streets only in California after the May incidents until late July, when the robotaxis resumed highway operations. In early July, Waymo told the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration that it began updating the robotaxi software to a version that “improve[s] the recognition of freeway construction zones, more appropriately prioritize[s] construction zones over other freeway hazards, and reduce[s] speed when the AV detects that it may be in a construction zone.” Read full article Comments
